entry.title: How We Built a Structured AI Readiness Assessment for SAP Customers - Stop Guessing. Start Assessing
entry.content:
Ask ten customers "how ready are you for AI?" and you get ten different answers — all of them based on gut feeling. Some point to a Copilot pilot that ran for three weeks. Others mention their data lake. A few say "we have an AI strategy" but can't tell you who owns it or what it covers. The result: conversations that start from completely different baselines, and recommendations that don't land.

That's the gap a structured AI Readiness Assessment closes.

We designed the assessment around nine dimensions — covering everything from executive strategy and workforce readiness to data foundation, technology infrastructure, and AI governance. Two dimensions are deliberately SAP-specific: the maturity of the SAP landscape itself, and whether there is an actual plan to consume and realize value from SAP's AI capabilities. Generic maturity frameworks miss exactly these.

Each dimension is scored 1–5: from L1 Initial (ad hoc, no structure) to L5 Autonomous Enterprise Ready (AI drives outcomes, full lifecycle in place). A score of 2 isn't a failure — it's a priority signal. What matters is the pattern across all nine axes: where is the organization strong, where is it lagging, and where are the critical gaps?

The assessment runs as a facilitated workshop, not a survey. When a cross-functional group has to agree on a number, the disagreements that surface are themselves a finding. That conversation produces three outputs.

The first is a radar chart — a 9-axis diagram showing current score in blue and target score in green for a 12–18 month horizon. The gap between the two lines is the prioritized action space.

The second is a gap analysis: for each dimension with a delta, concrete actions, ownership (SAP-side vs. customer-side), and effort classification — quick win or strategic initiative.


The third is a benchmark comparison — how does the customer's profile compare to peers at a similar transformation stage. This reframes the conversation from "are we good enough" to "where do we invest next to stay competitive."

 

The Tool Behind It
The assessment runs in a purpose-built Excel workbook with weighted scoring per dimension, plus a companion HTML visualization that renders the radar chart and gap analysis live during the session — no server, no login, no external dependency.

If you're working on something similar or want to adapt this for your own customer engagements, feel free to reach out.

entry.title: Architecting Digital Workforce: Understanding SAP Joule, Assistants, Agents, Skills and Joule studio
entry.content:
What if next generation of enterprise software is not about teaching people where to click, but about understanding what they are trying to accomplish? As an Enterprise Architect, this is the shift I find most interesting in the evolution of SAP Joule. 

For years, we have built business systems around applications, processes and transactions and people have had to learn how to navigate these systems to get their work done. But in real life, people start their day thinking about what they need to do, not which application they need to open.  A finance manager wants to resolve a payment issue. A procurement manager wants to solve a supplier problem. A sales manager wants to know which customer orders need attention. They all have one thing in common: they want to get the job done, without having to worry about the technology behind it.

AI gives us an opportunity to change how people work with enterprise systems. Instead of asking people to find their way through different applications, we can increasingly let them start by simply saying what they need.  That, to me, is where the story of Joule begins.

Joule: Bringing AI into the Flow of Business

What does Joule mean in this new way of working? I do not see Joule simply as another chatbot or another application that employees need to learn. I see it as an AI experience that helps people interact with their business more naturally. Joule can be embedded in SAP experiences where people already work, allowing them to ask questions, understand information and get help with business tasks without first having to figure out which application or transaction they need.

Imagine a finance professional dealing with a payment exception. Instead of starting by searching through different screens, the employee could ask, “Why is this payment blocked and what should I do next?” The conversation starts with the business problem, not with the technology behind it. From Enterprise Architecture perspective, this is an important shift: people can start with what they need, while Joule helps connect their request with relevant business information and capabilities.

What I find particularly valuable is the opportunity to bring AI closer to the work itself. Rather than making employees learn yet another tool, we can make interacting with enterprise systems more natural and help people focus on the decisions and outcomes that matter to their business.

Joule Assistants: Understanding the Business Behind the Request

Let us take our finance example a step further. Imagine an employee who needs help with a payment exception, such as a blocked payment. The employee is not just looking for a general answer; they need help with a specific business process. They need to understand what is happening, what information matters and what needs to be done next. This is where a Joule Assistant becomes important.

Joule Assistants for LOBs

Joule is the broader AI experience through which people interact with their business, while a Joule Assistant is designed around a particular business role or process. SAP's Finance portfolio, for example, includes specialized Assistants for Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Financial Closing, Cash and Treasury and other finance activities. Each focuses on a particular area of business work.

I find it helpful to think of it this way, Joule gives me a way to engage with my business, while the Assistant brings the right business context to my request. When the employee asks for help with a payment problem, the Accounts Payable Assistant can work within that finance context and coordinate the relevant Agents to move the work forward. For me, this is an important distinction: the goal is not simply to answer a question, but to understand the business need and help progress the work.

For more details, explore here  SAP Joule assistant for Finance 

Joule Agents : From Understanding to Execution

Once the Assistant understands the business context and coordinates what needs to happen, the next question is: who actually does the work? This is where Joule Agents come in.

Imagine the finance employee needs to investigate several payment exceptions. The work may involve checking payment details, looking at related invoices, gathering information from different systems and identifying what needs attention. This is more than answering a question; it involves several steps that need to come together to move the business problem forward. Joule Agents can work through such tasks by using the relevant data, tools and applications across SAP and third-party systems.

For me, the easiest way to understand the difference is that, the Assistant coordinates the work, while the Agent carries out the tasks needed to move it forward. Think of the Assistant as coordinating what needs to happen and the Agent as the digital worker that performs the required activities. Together, they can help turn a business request into meaningful action rather than leaving the employee to manage every step manually.

For more details, explore Joule agents 

Joule Skills: Giving the Agent the Capability

Now another question naturally follows: if an Agent is doing the work, how does it perform a specific task? This is where Joule Skills come in.

Let us return to our finance example. To investigate a blocked payment, an Agent may need to retrieve invoice details, check payment information, or perform a defined business operation. Each activity requires a specific capability. A Joule Skill provides that capability, with the instructions needed to perform the task. The Agent can use one or more Skills as it works towards the larger business objective.

Joule skills related response from Joule during development (RAG)

I find it helpful to think of it this way, the Agent works towards the goal, while a Skill helps it perform a specific task along the way. When these capabilities are well defined, they can be used as building blocks for more complex business activities. 

Joule Studio : From Business Intent to Enterprise-Ready AI

Every customer eventually reaches the same point: our business does not work exactly like everyone else’s. We have our own processes, industry requirements, applications, data and sometimes our own way of making decisions. So what happens when we need an AI capability that is specific to our business?

This is where Joule Studio becomes important. Joule Studio is SAP’s AI-first development environment for building custom AI Agents, applications and workflows, powered by the SAP Business AI Platform. It helps customers develop solutions tailored to their business requirements across SAP and non-SAP landscapes.

Returning to our finance example, imagine that the customer needs a custom AI Agent to support its particular process for handling blocked payments. With intent-based development, teams can describe their goals in natural language and Joule Studio can help turn those goals into development artifacts, such as technical specifications, code scaffolding and test artifacts. Once the solution is ready for deployment, the managed Joule Studio runtime provides a secure, production-ready environment without requiring customers to manage the underlying infrastructure themselves.

Intent-Driven Development decides whether you need a structured workflow or autonomous agent

Security and governance are equally important. The managed runtime supports isolated execution environments with configurable policies and guardrails, helping keep AI Agents within defined boundaries when interacting with enterprise systems.

From Enterprise Architecture perspective, this is an important part of the story. We are not limited to using predefined AI capabilities; we can build solutions around the way our own business operates. The goal is to connect business intent with the right processes, applications and AI capabilities to create a solution that fits the enterprise.

Get practice from Building Agents in Joule Studio - Step by Step 

Joule Work : A Workspace Built Around our business Goals

We have now explored Joule, Assistants, Agents, Skills and Joule Studio. But where can employees bring these capabilities together to get their work done? This is where Joule Work comes in.

Joule Work is a central, dynamic workspace that brings together relevant data, applications, insights and AI-powered workflows. Through Conversations, employees can express what they want to accomplish, while Spaces bring together the information, tools and context needed for a particular goal. The idea is to help people spend less time switching between applications and more time focusing on the work they need to get done.

Let us return to our finance example. An employee needs to investigate blocked payments. Through Joule Work, the employee can access relevant information and engage with the appropriate Joule Assistant. The Assistant uses the business-role and process context to coordinate the relevant Agents, which can carry out multi-step tasks across SAP and non-SAP systems using Joule Skills and other available tools.

Source: Architecture Center

The distinction is simple, Joule is SAP’s AI copilot that helps people interact with their business. Joule Work is the central workspace where people bring together the information and capabilities needed to achieve their goals. Within this experience, Assistants coordinate the work, Agents carry out multi-step tasks and Skills provide specific capabilities. Together, they help connect what people want to accomplish with the work needed to achieve it.

Bringing It All Together

Let us return to the finance use case. Our finance expert has a payment problem and expresses the business need through Joule. The relevant Joule Assistant understands the finance context and coordinates the work that needs to happen. Joule Agents carry out the required tasks, using Joule Skills for specific activities along the way. If the customer needs a capability tailored to its own business processes, it can build and extend it through Joule Studio. Meanwhile, Joule Work brings the relevant information, applications and AI-powered workflows together in one workspace.

Our finance expert does not need to understand how all these components work behind the scenes. That is the point: technology should make work simpler.

From Enterprise Architecture perspective, the real opportunity is not to make people understand more technology, but to help them focus on the business outcomes they need to achieve. When AI connects business intent with the right context and capabilities, the enterprise experience can become more natural and the work easier to accomplish.

They simply need to say: “I have a business problem. Help me solve it.”

Disclaimer:  I humbly share these insights as a reflection of my personal understanding and point of view.

entry.title: SuccessConnect 2026: Joule Agents Are Here. Is Your SAP SuccessFactors Architecture Ready?
entry.content:
My firsthand view from Las Vegas: the breakthroughs, the real availability status, and the technical questions that matter after the keynote.

Three days at SuccessConnect in Las Vegas convinced me of one thing: the next test for SAP SuccessFactors is not whether AI can answer an HR question. It is whether an agent can take the right action, in the right system, with the right permission, and leave enough evidence for us to trust the result.

I was in the audience when Siva Sundaresan walked through the expanding Joule Assistant portfolio. On the screen was a dense slide labelled “Available this month.” Another was labelled “Coming soon.” I photographed both.

They looked like product-roadmap slides. To me, they looked like an architecture review waiting to happen.

Configuration Transport Agent. Role-Based Permissions Agent. HCM Audit Agent. Skills Governance Agent. Payroll Alert Resolution Agent. Winston recruiting capabilities. Onboarding Task Management.

Each name suggests a task an HR technology team knows well. Each also raises a less glamorous question: what happens when the agent needs to change something?

At SAP Connect 2026, Christian Klein connected the Autonomous Enterprise vision across business functions. In the SuccessFactors keynote, Siva brought that ambition into Plan, Hire, Manage, Pay, Develop, and Grow.

I spent time with Joule Studio and followed the demonstrations and roadmap discussions. The announcements were substantial. But the most important takeaway from my three days was not a count of agents.

My thesis: agentic HCM shifts complexity from navigating screens to governing decisions and actions across systems.

That is where the real customer value and the real implementation risk now sit.

1. The breakthrough isn't a better chatbot. It's a different unit of work.

We have spent years building HR landscapes around transactions: create a position, approve a requisition, update a job record, assign learning, investigate an exception.

Each transaction has its place in a process, usually with handoffs between teams and applications.

Autonomous HCM starts from a different question: what outcome is the business trying to achieve?

Siva described three connected pillars:

  • Automate: Reduce repetitive work.
  • Redesign: Change how people and AI perform work together.
  • Reinvent: Rethink how organizations recruit, develop, move, and reward their workforce.

SAP also discussed 20 outcome-oriented opportunities across the employee lifecycle.

Those are important distinctions. Automating a weak process does not make it a good process.

Take a business request for ten additional specialists.

Today's response may be ten requisitions. Tomorrow's better question might be whether the business needs ten hires, some redeployment, targeted learning, contingent capacity, or a redesign of the underlying work.

That requires organizational data, financial context, skills evidence, and an understanding of what the business actually does.

For an HR architect, the difference is profound.

A system can execute a well-defined transaction. An outcome often crosses several systems of record.

We are not removing the integration problem. We are moving it behind a simpler experience.

2. Three agents I would put through a real customer test

I am deliberately starting with technical administration, not the flashiest employee demo.

These are scenarios in which an incorrect action can be expensive, even when the conversation looks convincing.

Test A: Configuration Transport Agent. Can it move a change without losing control?

In a typical DEV-QAS-PROD landscape, a successful transport depends on more than selecting an object and clicking Import.

We need to know what changed, what depends on it, whether the target is ready, and how the business process will be tested afterward.

SAP's learning documentation describes an agent that can:

  • Search configuration changes by date, modifier, and area.
  • Create or update transport bundles.
  • Initiate transport and request validation.
  • Guide an administrator through import.
  • Present validation findings, including warnings and errors.

For a selected bundle, SAP describes checks around validation status, dependencies, and maintenance-window considerations before import.

Search results that require asynchronous reporting include a freshness indicator and are retained for 24 hours.

That is considerably more useful than a chatbot that merely explains Configuration Transport Center.

My acceptance test: Modify a controlled Employee Central or platform configuration in DEV. Ask the agent to locate the change, create a bundle, review what it included, move it to QAS, and inspect validation warnings.

Then confirm the outcome against the native transport record and execute the actual business-process regression test.

What would make me reject the result?

A bundle that silently picks up unrelated changes, an unexplained dependency warning, missing authorization boundaries, or a success message that is mistaken for end-to-end functional validation.

Availability check: SAP Learning currently labels the HR System Assistant and Configuration Transport Agent as Early Adopter Care (EAC). The “Available this month” keynote slide should not be interpreted as universal tenant availability.

Test B: Role-Based Permissions Agent. Does it solve the right access problem?

Consider a manager who cannot access an organizational feature.

In RBP, the answer can involve a permission, role, permission group, role assignment, and target population.

Granting broader access can make the immediate complaint disappear while introducing a security problem.

SAP documents an agent that can investigate why a user lacks access, list roles and permissions, identify who has a specific permission, and propose a fix with reasoning and impact information.

In a supported case, it can add a user to a static permission group after confirmation.

It is also currently in EAC.

My acceptance test: Reproduce a known access issue with a test user. Ask for the diagnosis, compare the explanation with the actual role-assignment chain, and inspect the scope of the proposed fix before approving any change.

One question matters more than how quickly the agent responds:

Did it restore the intended access without granting more than the user needs?

Test C: HCM Audit Agent. Can it show the evidence, not merely an answer?

Imagine a sensitive employee field changed unexpectedly.

A support analyst may need Change Audit, Read Audit, login activity, and proxy-session context to understand what happened.

SAP describes the HCM Audit Agent correlating Change, Read, and General Audit sources to investigate data changes, permissions, access to sensitive information, login events, and proxy activity.

This is potentially valuable because the investigation crosses evidence sources that an administrator would otherwise examine separately.

There is a fundamental boundary:

The agent can report only what the underlying audit logs captured.

It does not manufacture missing evidence. It is also documented as EAC.

My acceptance test: Perform a controlled change and a permitted read of test data. Establish the expected audit records first, then ask the agent to reconstruct the event timeline.

Evaluate source traceability, omissions, timestamps, and access restrictions, not just the quality of its narrative.

Across these three tests, I would measure four things: accuracy, time saved, permission discipline, and the ability to reconstruct what the agent did.

That is a much stronger business case than “we enabled three agents.”

3. Recruiting makes the architecture problem impossible to ignore

SmartRecruiters and SuccessFactors offer a useful way to think about end-to-end agentic work because the process naturally crosses application boundaries.

Consider this illustrative implementation scenario, not a claim about a particular keynote demo:

  1. A position is approved in SAP SuccessFactors Employee Central.
  2. A recruiting requisition is created and managed in SmartRecruiters.
  3. Winston capabilities assist the recruiting team with supported matching, screening, interview, or knowledge activities.
  4. After the hiring decision and required approvals, the supported handoff initiates the next hiring and onboarding steps.
  5. Downstream systems receive the appropriate worker information at the correct point in the lifecycle.

On paper, it is one hiring outcome.

Technically, it contains multiple records, owners, statuses, identities, and failure modes.

If the position changes after requisition creation, which information can be updated, and where?

If the offer is withdrawn after a downstream event is triggered, what is the reversal or correction path?

If a candidate is a rehire, which matching and person-identity rules determine the right employee record?

If an event is retried, how do we avoid duplicates?

These are ordinary integration design questions. Agents do not remove them.

In some cases, they make them more urgent because users may perceive the experience as a single continuous workflow.

SAP's October SmartRecruiters implementation guidance is a useful reminder: SmartRecruiters can be deployed without Employee Central, but that changes the availability of productized master-data synchronization, position-led hiring, and standard hire handoff.

An agent-enabled experience cannot be assumed to erase those product boundaries.

The recruiting portfolio shown at SuccessConnect included Winston Companion, Interview, Chat, Match, and other capabilities.

But an assistant name is not an integration specification.

Before committing to a design, customers still need to verify the supported actions, APIs, ownership of each object, the required identity model, and the lifecycle events actually delivered by the product.

This is also why I separate candidate-facing experiences from employee- or recruiter-facing Joule experiences.

Authentication, privacy, and permitted actions differ by audience.

4. TechWolf changes the workforce conversation, but not overnight

One of the biggest announcements came as Day 2 began: SAP had entered into an agreement to acquire TechWolf.

For me, this was not simply another AI acquisition headline.

It addresses a problem I see at the intersection of workforce planning and Talent Intelligence Hub:

Organizations often know which jobs exist, but not enough about the work people actually perform.

TechWolf's Context Graph for Work is designed to build a continuously updated view of tasks, applied skills, and labor-market context using connected business and HR data.

That could improve the evidence behind decisions on hiring, internal mobility, reskilling, and role redesign.

Now connect that direction with SAP's announced Workforce Planning Assistant.

SAP plans for it to combine SuccessFactors workforce data, SAP Fieldglass contingent-labor information, and SAP Cloud ERP financial information through SAP Enterprise Planning.

The ambition is to recommend a more effective mix of hiring, redeployment, reskilling, and external talent.

Here is the non-obvious implication:

An organization may have to improve its job architecture before its workforce intelligence becomes useful.

A poor role taxonomy or inconsistent skills definitions cannot be repaired merely by presenting the information through Joule.

SAP's Job Architecture Maintenance Agent makes that dependency concrete.

Its published learning material describes comparing Job Profile Builder role definitions with skills from Growth Portfolio and job requisitions, identifying missing role-skill mappings and orphaned roles, and proposing updates for administrator confirmation.

Job Profile Builder and Talent Intelligence Hub are stated prerequisites.

This agent is also identified as EAC.

That gives HRIT teams an actionable starting point today: audit role quality, verify position mappings, review skills governance, and identify stale or orphaned job structures before expecting sophisticated workforce recommendations.

 Timing matters: As of October 9, the TechWolf transaction is an agreement, not a completed acquisition. SAP expects closing in Q4 2026 subject to customary conditions, including regulatory approval.

The Workforce Planning Assistant is targeted for EAC in Q4 2026.

The future integrated experience should be treated as direction, not delivered functionality.

5. The quieter Employee Central and Learning announcements matter too

Not everything valuable at SuccessConnect appeared in a Joule conversation.

Organizational Modeling: Test the prerequisites before the simulation

SAP's 2H 2026 Organizational Modeling capability lets authorized users model changes to organizational units and positions rather than directly manipulating the live structure without a planning view.

 Initial operations include creating, editing, moving, deactivating, or deleting supported organizational objects, subject to the documented scope.

The implementation detail matters:

SAP identifies Employee Central Position Management with Position-to-Job Information synchronization as a prerequisite.

Access combines SuccessFactors RBP with groups in SAP Cloud Identity Services.

A customer without a solid position model or consistent identity administration should solve those problems before assessing the modeling experience.

Role-Based Document View: Practical value, with boundaries

The new Documents category in the latest People Profile aims to consolidate supported employee-related documents in one place, subject to existing RBP.

It also offers in-system preview for common document formats, reducing unnecessary local downloads.

But this is an access experience, not a replacement for full document management.

SAP documents exclusions, including certain dependent-related and uncategorized documents, as well as limits on managing files from that view.

Customers need to test what each persona can actually see.

Benefits and Learning: Fewer steps only matter if the result is reliable

SAP announced an agentic administration console for U.S. benefits, targeted for general availability in Q4 2026, and U.S. Benefits Decision Support, targeted for Q1 2027.

The first focuses on enrollment oversight and exceptions. The second aims to bring contextual recommendations into employee enrollment choices.

For Learning, the planned WalkMe Learning Arc integration with SAP SuccessFactors Learning is targeted for general availability in December 2026.

The concept is to generate courses and quizzes from natural-language learning requirements while keeping the author in control.

These experiences should be evaluated against the same standard as an agent: does the workflow improve while eligibility, review, privacy, localization, and audit requirements remain intact?

One slide I captured looked further ahead: “Gemini Notebook in SuccessFactors” with a 2027 marker under the theme “The Knowledge Canvas Meets the System of Record.”

Its value proposition, less searching and more context-rich HR work, is intriguing.

But I would label it exactly as the conference presented it: a future-facing concept, not a capability to plan as generally available today.

 6. Joule Studio was exciting. The production checklist was more exciting.

I spent time in the hands-on Joule Studio discussions, including an example that connected agent creation with an n8n-based workflow.

The speed of moving from a natural-language requirement toward an orchestrated solution was compelling.

Christian Klein's keynote placed that in the larger Joule Work experience:

  • Conversations: Questions and delegation.
  • Spaces: Contextual work.
  • Joule Studio: Extending and building solutions.

SAP also positioned AI Agent Hub and Business AI Platform governance as part of the operating model across agents and underlying tools.

For me, the interesting question began after the prototype worked.

If an agent changes a job record, what identity does the transaction use?

If a connected service fails halfway through, does the workflow retry, halt, or require a human decision?

Where can the support team see the tool calls and resulting business transactions?

Who owns the agent after the project team leaves?

Here is the architecture review I would use before allowing a custom HR agent into production:

Control Question to answer Evidence I would require

System ownershipWhich application owns each object and transaction?Object-level source-of-truth and supported-action map
Identity and authorizationWhose rights are used when the agent acts?Execution-identity design, permission scope, approval path
Failure and recoveryWhat happens after a partial completion or retry?Failure tests, idempotency design where applicable, support runbook
Audit and observabilityCan we reconstruct what was requested and changed?Correlated logs, transaction references, evidence-retention policy
Human controlWhich operations require confirmation or escalation?Risk-tiered controls with tested stop and override mechanisms

This is not a claim that any single SAP agent automatically implements every control in the table.

It is the standard I would apply when assessing a customer-specific agentic process.

Prototype speed is not production readiness. In HR, the evidence of a correct action matters as much as the action itself.

7. The HCM keynote was only half the architecture story

Re-reading SAP's official Innovation News Guide after Las Vegas, I found something that strengthened my original takeaway:

Some of the announcements most relevant to an HR architect sit outside the HCM chapter.

They address the four things an agent needs before it can be trusted to act: a consistent understanding of the data, a bounded identity, a supported connection to the next system, and a way to measure its impact.

One employee, several records: Why SAP Reltio matters

Employee and worker information often appears in Employee Central, recruiting, contingent-workforce, finance, and identity systems, each with its own identifiers and timing.

An agent cannot resolve those differences just because its answer sounds confident.

SAP announced SAP Reltio in SAP Business Data Cloud to reconcile fragmented entities across SAP and non-SAP applications and provide a shared system of context.

SAP states the solution is generally available now.

This does not replace Employee Central as the employee system of record.

The architectural question is how the agent obtains consistent context while approved source systems retain ownership of transactions.

Governance must include the agent's identity, not only the employee's

The guide introduces an Access Governance and Security Assistant designed to extend identity governance across human and AI identities, alongside a Governance Assistant that correlates risk signals across systems.

That directly reinforces my RBP acceptance test.

Knowing who asked is not sufficient.

We must know what the agent was permitted to do, under which identity and approval boundary, and what evidence remains afterward.

SAP plans general availability for:

  • Access Governance and Security Assistant: Q1 2027.
  • Governance Assistant: Q4 2026.

Those are roadmap targets, not capabilities to presume active in a current HR tenant.

A process does not stop at Employee Central

Two other announcements deserve attention.

The Contingent Workforce Assistant aims to connect HR and procurement activities across contingent-worker hiring, approvals, exceptions, and offboarding, with general availability planned for Q4 2026.

Separately, SAP announced expanded SAP-managed integration between SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and SAP SuccessFactors, targeted for Q4 2026 availability.

Neither announcement means every existing custom integration disappears.

The exact delivered process, supported objects, endpoints, and commercial prerequisites will determine what it can replace in a customer's architecture.

We will need evidence of adoption and value, too

SAP also announced Signavio AI agent mining to help analyze agent workflows, conformance, and performance, with availability planned for Q1 2027.

Meanwhile, its new WalkMe AI insights and AI authoring capabilities are described as generally available now.

I see these as different but complementary measures.

One asks whether agent-driven processes work as intended. The other helps identify where people struggle and create guidance.

Neither is a substitute for verifying a transaction against the underlying system.

The lesson: Agent readiness is not only a SuccessFactors feature checklist.

It spans data context, human and agent identities, integration ownership, process observability, and adoption.

That is a more realistic definition of the Autonomous Enterprise than a tally of agents on a keynote slide.

8. What is really available? Read the roadmap twice.

My photographs capture the excitement of the October portfolio, but they also illustrate why availability needs careful wording.

A slide headed “Available this month” is not the same as a tenant-specific entitlement and activation check.

SAP's Innovation News Guide says general availability for the expanding portfolio starts in October, while its learning material explicitly identifies some HR System capabilities as EAC-only.

Area Announced availability / status

Joule WorkOctober rollout announced; customer enablement and scope require verification.
HR System Assistant, RBP, Transport, HCM AuditEarly Adopter Care in SAP Learning documentation.
Other keynote HCM agentsOctober-targeted and future capabilities vary; verify each individually.
Workforce Planning AssistantEAC planned Q4 2026.
TechWolfAcquisition agreement announced; Q4 2026 close expected, subject to conditions.
WalkMe Learning Arc integrationGeneral availability planned December 2026.
U.S. Benefits Administration ConsoleGeneral availability planned Q4 2026.
U.S. Benefits Decision SupportGeneral availability planned Q1 2027.
Gemini Notebook in SuccessFactors2027 roadmap indication from conference slide; no GA claim.
SAP Reltio, Business Data CloudGenerally available now.
Access Governance and Security AssistantGeneral availability planned Q1 2027.
Governance AssistantGeneral availability planned Q4 2026.
Contingent Workforce AssistantGeneral availability planned Q4 2026.
SAP-managed S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and SuccessFactors integrationGeneral availability planned Q4 2026 for supported scenarios.
SAP Signavio AI agent miningGeneral availability planned Q1 2027.
WalkMe AI insights and authoringGenerally available now.

My rule is simple:

Announce the vision, but implement against the documented release.

Licensing, country scope, product prerequisites, permissions, tenant enablement, and supported actions remain separate checks.

9. My 30-day action plan for HRIT leaders and SuccessFactors architects

I would not leave SuccessConnect with a plan to “enable AI across HR.”

I would leave with a plan to test one outcome properly.

Week 1: Pick the workflow, not the agent

Choose one recurring issue, such as RBP access troubleshooting, transport validation, or payroll exception investigation.

Record the current turnaround time, rework, approvals, and common errors.

Week 2: Map the boundaries

Document objects, systems of record, relevant users, RBP and identity controls, integration dependencies, and exception states.

Confirm current SAP availability and entitlement before scheduling an agent trial.

Explicitly map any agent identity, cross-system identifier reconciliation, and whether an interface uses SAP-managed or customer-maintained integration.

Week 3: Run a non-production acceptance test

Include a successful path, missing data, unauthorized access, a failed downstream call where relevant, and a retry.

Compare each outcome with the native system and audit evidence.

Week 4: Make a measured decision

Calculate time saved and error rates, review control gaps, name the service owner, and decide whether to expand, redesign, or defer.

Do not count a successful demo as a successful deployment.

The measure that matters is not how many agents appear on the launch dashboard.

It is whether an HR process became faster or more reliable without weakening the controls people depend on.

The question I brought home from Las Vegas

There was a lot to absorb at SuccessConnect 2026: Autonomous HCM, the TechWolf announcement, Winston and recruiting innovation, Joule Work, agent governance, new Employee Central capabilities, and hands-on agent development.

But the most revealing moments for me were the ones that connected AI to the unglamorous realities of running HR systems.

Moving configuration. Investigating access. Tracing an audit event. Keeping job architecture current. Handing a new hire correctly from one application to another.

That is where the promise will be tested.

When an agent says “Done,” can you tell what changed, in which system, under whose authority, and how to recover if something went wrong?

If the answer is yes, agentic HR has begun to move beyond the keynote.

If the answer is no, we have only made the interface look simpler.

That is my biggest takeaway from SuccessConnect 2026, and the standard I will use when evaluating Joule agents in real SAP SuccessFactors landscapes.

entry.title: How Account Synopsis and Executive Summary Work in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2
entry.content:
Smarter Account Intelligence in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2: Account Synopsis and Executive Summary

 

Why Account Context is Still a CX Problem

A seller has a customer meeting in 15 minutes.

The account record contains years of activity history, open opportunities, service interactions, stakeholder changes, and strategic account planning data.

Everything the seller needs is technically available, but finding what matters is a different challenge.

Meanwhile, on the service side, an agent picks up a call from a long-standing customer. The case history is there. The contracts are there. But the agent has no idea what this company actually does, what market they operate in, or whether there is an upsell opportunity sitting right in front of them.

This is one of the most common problems in modern customer-facing organizations; whether sales or service. Teams rarely struggle because they lack data. They struggle because important context is scattered across multiple sources and requires time to complete the puzzle.

As a result:

  • New account managers spend weeks getting up to speed.
  • Sales reps walk into meetings with incomplete context.
  • Service agents handle interactions without understanding the customer’s broader business.
  • Strategic account reviews become exercises in information gathering rather than strategy.
  • The gap is no longer data availability, but understanding.

This is exactly where Account Synopsis and Account Plan Executive Summary in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 enter the picture. Both use Generative AI to reduce the effort required to understand an account; yet they solve different problems, and they serve different audiences.

 

Two Features. Two Different Questions.

A useful way to understand these capabilities is to focus on the business question each one answers.

Account Synopsis

Account Synopsis answers: "Who is this customer and what is happening in their world?"

It combines publicly available company information with account master data to create a quick business briefing directly inside the Account record. The key word here is external: this feature reaches beyond your CRM to pull in market intelligence you would otherwise spend time Googling.

Account Synopsis is available in both SAP Sales Cloud V2 and SAP Service Cloud V2, but the use case differs by role:

  • For sales reps, it is a meeting preparation tool: building account context before discovery sessions, executive introductions, and account handovers.
  • For service agents, it is a real-time context layer: surfaced during customer interactions to help agents facilitate targeted conversations and identify upsell or cross-sell opportunities on the spot.

Account Plan Executive Summary (Sales Cloud V2 Only)

The Executive Summary answers: "What is our strategy for this account and how are we progressing?"

Instead of relying on external company information, it looks inward. It uses Account Plan content already maintained inside Sales Cloud: goals, SWOT analyses, action plans, business figures, and pipeline information to generate a concise strategic narrative.

This feature is specific to SAP Sales Cloud V2, because it is tied to Account Plans: a concept that lives in the sales planning workflow. It is not available in Service Cloud V2.

This makes it valuable for:

  • Quarterly Business Reviews
  • Strategic account reviews
  • Leadership briefings
  • Customer planning sessions

 

Where These Features Sit in SAP’s AI Strategy

SAP’s AI portfolio within Sales and Service Cloud V2 includes predictive Machine Learning, Generative AI capabilities, and the emerging layer of AI agents. Account Synopsis and Executive Summary sit firmly within the Generative AI category because their purpose is not prediction. Their purpose is synthesis.

Instead of trying to forecast future outcomes, they transform large amounts of information into structured narratives that humans can consume quickly. The goal is not to tell a seller or service agent what decision to make, but to help them reach a decision faster.

Both features are delivered as part of the Joule Premium for Customer Experience package and are embedded into SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 AI capabilities.

In practical terms: the intelligence behind these features is not some standalone AI experiment. It is deeply wired into the platform you are already using, whether that platform serves your sales team, your service team, or both.

 

A Closer Look at Account Synopsis

Opening an Account Synopsis generates a structured view of the customer across several configurable dimensions. Administrators can choose which of the following to expose to users:

  • Overall Information
  • Business Overview
  • Typical Customers
  • Competitive Landscape
  • Culture and Background
  • Business Strategies

 

 

Together, these sections create a quick overview of the organization that goes well beyond what is typically stored in CRM records. The AI consumes external, publicly available data about the company in real-time, delivering market intelligence as a structured synopsis directly in a dedicated AI Synopsis tab within the Account detail view. Each generation or regeneration counts as one AI unit transaction.

Sales Cloud and Service Cloud: Where the Value Lands

In SAP Sales Cloud V2, Account Synopsis is primarily a preparation tool. Sales reps use it before meetings, during account handovers, and as part of discovery sessions.

The value is measured in time saved during account planning: SAP’s benchmarks show a reduction from 60 minutes to 30 minutes per account review.

In SAP Service Cloud V2, the same synopsis is surfaced directly to service agents during live customer interactions. Here, the value is different: it is about enabling targeted conversations and spotting cross-sell or upsell opportunities in real-time. SAP’s published metrics point to a 2% increase in cross-sell and upsell revenue for service FTEs.

 

The Account Plan Executive Summary (Sales Cloud V2)

Many organizations invest significant time maintaining goals, SWOT analyses, revenue targets, action plans, and strategic initiatives, only to create separate documents when leadership reviews or QBRs arrive. If that sounds familiar, you are not alone.

The Executive Summary addresses this problem. Available exclusively in SAP Sales Cloud V2, it converts structured planning information into a concise narrative that can be reviewed, edited, and shared directly from within the Account Plan.

The generated output is organized around four themes:

Account Overview A summary of the customer relationship, strategic positioning, and business objectives.

Customer Priorities and Our Response An explanation of customer goals and how the organization is addressing them.

Risks and Challenges Known risks, dependencies, and potential obstacles.

What’s Upcoming Future engagements and relevant pipeline information.

 

How to Trigger It

Users navigate to Account Plans → open a plan → select the Executive Summary tab → choose “Generate Summary.” The result is an editable draft that can be copied to clipboard for external use. If a summary was previously generated, it can be viewed or regenerated.

Unlike Account Synopsis, the Executive Summary is fully editable. Users can refine the content, add business context, and save the final version directly inside the plan.

 

 

The following figures come from SAP’s Business AI Value Calculator (v3.6, June 2026) and published product pages on the SAP Discovery Center. These are SAP-validated benchmarks based on VLM (Value Lifecycle Management) benchmarks and SAP Expert Estimation.

Yes, you read that correctly! The annual AI running cost is €6,246 against a total annual benefit of over €2.6 million. That is not a typo. That is the kind of ROI that makes finance teams do a double take.

The service-side value proposition is less about time savings and more about revenue capture. When agents understand the customer’s business context during a live interaction, they are better positioned to identify opportunities that would otherwise be invisible.

 

In the Field: Döhler’s Story

The most publicly documented live deployment is Döhler, a global food and beverage ingredients company with approximately 9,500 employees, €640 million+ in revenue, 3,000+ CRM users, and 27,600 customers. Döhler went live on SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 globally in Q3 2025.

Key facts from their deployment:

  • Account Synopsis is live in production alongside Lead Booster, Lead Intelligence/Scoring, Deal Scoring, Case Summary, Case Classification, and Similar Case Recommendation.
  • Integration with OpenAI was used to enrich leads and accounts, with market insights such as product shortages surfaced automatically.
  • The system delivers "exceptional loading speed and system responsiveness" with "virtually no loading times" even on large account/opportunity objects.

"The usability, performance and productivity gains are excellent. We are excited to deploy SAP’s Sales and Service Cloud V2 in 2025 expanding on the exceptional value to IT, end users, customers and suppliers."

— Vasiliki Galani, Lead IT & Market Functions, Döhler

 

Prerequisites and Licensing

Before activating these features, there are a few practical items to check off. This is the part of the article that saves you a support ticket.

Licensing: Both features require a valid SAP AI Units license: specifically the Joule Premium for Customer Experience package. This applies whether you are using Account Synopsis in Sales Cloud V2, Service Cloud V2, or both. Customers must raise an incident with component CEC-CRM-ML confirming their license to enable the features.

Role Assignment: Users need the sap.crm.service.mlScenarioManagementGenAIService role assignment.

Language Support: Generative AI features are tested and supported for English, German, French, and Spanish. Use in other languages is untested and may produce unreliable results. Human review is recommended.

AI Unit Consumption: Each Account Synopsis generation counts as one transaction. Every regeneration also counts as a separate transaction. The same applies to other GenAI features like Lead Booster, Email Drafter, and Survey Trend Summary.

⚠️Note: The Joule Premium for Customer Experience per-user-per-month SKU is currently being retired, as SAP is moving these features into Base AI. If you are signing a new contract or renewing, confirm with your SAP Account Executive whether Account Synopsis is covered under your Base AI entitlement or still requires a separate AI Units purchase before raising an activation incident.

 

Final Thoughts

The most successful AI capabilities in enterprise software are often the least disruptive.

They do not change how people work. They improve how quickly people can work.

Account Synopsis and Account Plan Executive Summary follow that principle.

Account Synopsis helps both sellers and service agents understand the customer’s world.

Executive Summary helps account teams communicate their strategy.

Neither replaces experience. Neither replaces account knowledge. And neither removes the need for good data.

But when implemented in the right environment with clean data, clear processes, and realistic expectations: both can reduce the distance between information and understanding.

Besides, if an AI can save you from one more “So... tell me about your company” moment - whether you are a seller in a boardroom or an agent on a call - I would say it has already earned its keep.

What is SAP Joule, and where can I get the latest information on Joule?
We update constantly the official documentation of SAP Joule, and you can always refer to the official documentation here.

What are the different types of skills that Joule is capable of?

  • Navigational. Users can ask Joule to help navigate and open the correct FIORI apps and SAP transactions to perform certain business processes.
  • Transactional. Joule can understand the questions and retrieve the necessary business data from the backend SAP system and react on the user instructions to trigger executable steps directly in the backend systems.
  • Analytical. Joule can provide real time analytical views on certain business processes and steps within SAP systems.

In the following paragraphs, we provide a breakdown of each Joule skill.

Joule informational skills in EWM
As part of the centrally delivered Joule skills, it understands automatically also the EWM context and business objects based on trained SAP help documentation. entry.title: t's All Joule Everywhere, Do You Actually Know Which Joule You are Talking About?
entry.content:
t's All Joule Everywhere, Do You Actually Know Which Joule You are Talking About?

Spend any time in the SAP ecosystem right now and you will hear one word more than any other and its Joule

Joule in SuccessFactors. Joule Work. Joule Agents. Joule Assistants. Joule Studio. It's on every slide in every keynote, in every product update. 

"Are these all the same thing? Are they different products? What does each one actually do, and which one do I actually need?"

Let's break it down.

Before the classification, it's worth asking: why does this family even exist?

For decades, enterprise software was designed around a fundamental assumption: users learn the system. You train people to navigate menus, find features, run reports, follow workflows. The system was the authority and users adapted to it.

The result? Feature-rich platforms where most users only ever discover 20% of the capability. Time-off requests, performance forms and policy questions are all buried inside screens that require navigation, training and patience.

The Joule Family: A Clear Classification

Think of the Joule family as a layered stack each layer serving a distinct purpose, all working together

Layer 1 — Joule (The Umbrella AI Experience)

What it is: Joule is SAP's overarching AI copilot and engagement layer. It is "the broader AI experience through which people interact with their business.

The need it addresses: Users need a single, consistent AI presence across SAP regardless of which module, which device, or which process they are working in. Joule is that presence.

Its function: Joule answers questions, provides recommendations, helps users navigate to the right application, and surfaces insights drawn from SAP and connected third-party data. It is grounded in the SAP Knowledge Graph, which maps more than 7 million data fields across the SAP portfolio giving it real business context, not generic AI responses.

Layer 2 — Joule Assistants (The Orchestrators)

What they are: Joule Assistants are purpose-built for a specific business role or process. They go beyond answering questions they coordinate the work that needs to happen within a defined business context.

The need they address: Generic AI can answer questions. But HR work is contextual. A payroll query and a workforce planning request are very different they need different data, different logic, different guardrails. Joule Assistants bring that role-specific intelligence.

its function: "The Assistant coordinates the work, while the Agent carries out the tasks needed to move it forward." Assistants understand the nuances of a process, surface the right context

Layer 3 — Joule Agents (The Executors)

What they are: Joule Agents are the doers. They execute multi-step tasks autonomously across systems, across data sources, within the boundaries set by your organisation's existing authorisations, rules and audit trails.

The need they address: Orchestration without execution is just planning. Once an Assistant decides what needs to happen, something has to do it update a record, trigger a workflow, move a configuration, generate a document across potentially multiple systems in sequence.

Their function: Agents carry out specific, bounded tasks. Critically, they operate within your existing governance they don't bypass permissions or create shadow workflows. SAP's framing is deliberate: "Agents operate within established data, authorisations, and audit trails to maintain control."

Layer 4 — Joule Work (The Workspace / UI)

What it is: Joule Work is the new unified interface "the new UI for AI" where employees and HR teams actually engage with all of the above. Launched at SAP Connect 2026 and rolling out to all customers in October 2026.

The need it addresses: Having powerful Assistants and Agents is only useful if people can actually reach them intuitively. Joule Work solves the access and discoverability problem it replaces navigation-first interaction with intent-first interaction.

Its function: Joule Work is built on three pillars:

  • Conversations - Users express what they want in natural language. Joule Work interprets the intent, engages the right Assistant, and gets the work done.
  • Spaces - Dynamic, shared work areas that surface the content, data, insights, and applications relevant to a goal - across SAP and non-SAP sources. Think of a Workforce Planning Space that brings together headcount data, open roles, skills gaps, and budget in one view.
  • Develop (Joule Studio) - The build capability, directly accessible within Joule Work, where teams extend or create their own agents and workflows.

 

Layer 5 — Joule Studio (The Build Layer)

 

What it is: Joule Studio is SAP's AI-first development environment. It enables business users and IT professionals to create, customise and govern AI agents and workflows from no-code to pro-code.

The need it addresses: No out-of-the-box agent library covers every organisation's unique HR processes. Companies need the ability to extend Joule to fit their specific workflows, policies, and data structures without building from scratch on a separate platform.

Its function: Joule Studio lets you describe what you want to build in plain language it translates your intent into product requirements and technical specifications, then helps implement the solution. Agents built in Studio can reason across SAP and non-SAP systems, invoke APIs, and integrate into governed enterprise workflows.

 

How It All Fits Together Here's the mental model that I find most useful:

You INTERACT in     →  Joule Work       (the workspace)

You TALK TO         →  Joule            (the AI experience)

It COORDINATES via  →  Joule Assistants (the orchestrators)

It EXECUTES via     →  Joule Agents     (the doers)

You CUSTOMISE with  →  Joule Studio     (the builder)

entry.title: Building Custom Assistants and Agents for Asset Management in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition
entry.content:
What we built and why
I recently worked on a custom Asset Health Assistant, built as an AI agent connected to SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition (SAP Cloud ERP). The assistant uses Joule's agent capabilities together with MCP (Model Context Protocol) to access live asset management data through a conversational interface.
The idea was straightforward: let a maintenance supervisor or plant manager ask questions in plain language and get structured answers directly from the system. No report building. No navigation. Just a question and an answer grounded in real operational data.
What the assistant actually does
To give a sense of what this looks like in practice, here is a summary of the kinds of questions we explored during a session focused on the Atlanta Bottling Facility and several other plants across the US.
 
Failure pattern analysis: The assistant retrieved the top five equipment categories with the most frequent failures at the Atlanta Bottling Facility in 2026. The counts were tightly clustered, which pointed to systemic maintenance challenges rather than a single weak point.
Cross-facility comparisons: We asked which equipment had experienced valve failures across both Dallas Manufacturing Facility and Atlanta Bottling Facility.
Atlanta showed a much broader spread, with valve failures affecting all five production lines across every major equipment category. That kind of pattern is hard to spot when you are looking at one facility at a time.

Failure code consistency: The assistant showed that the capper equipment category in Georgia and Texas shares an identical set of eight failure codes.
This suggests that capper failures are driven by common equipment design or maintenance practices, not by location-specific conditions.
 
Maintenance strategy review: We looked at average time between maintenance for cycle-based strategies on specific equipment types in Dallas.
The Crown Capper averaged 202.9 hours (~8.5 days) between maintenance; the Pressure Sensitive Labeler averaged 150.9 hours (~6.3 days). These numbers give a starting point for evaluating whether intervals align with actual failure patterns.

Work order backlogs: The assistant surfaced all Reactive work orders in "In Process" status for LINE1 across Atlanta and Los Angeles.

Atlanta had at least 17 open corrective orders on a single line, which signals a meaningful reactive maintenance backlog.

Condition-based maintenance plans: For pump equipment in Dallas, the assistant retrieved 10 condition-based maintenance plans, including their status breakdown.
Four were still in "Created" status (planned but not started), and one had been in process since September 2024, suggesting scheduling delays.

OEE by production shift:The assistant calculated OEE metrics for each shift at Atlanta Bottling Facility.
The Afternoon Shift had the highest downtime (375 hours), with valve failure as the primary cause. The Night Shift's leading issue was sensor malfunction. The Weekend Shift saw a combination of hydraulic leaks and electrical issues. Performance scores across all shifts hovered in the 83 to 84 percent range, below world-class benchmarks.

Downtime event deep dives: When comparing Afternoon Shift downtime events between Dallas and Atlanta, the gap was significant.
Atlanta recorded 3,100 events compared to 1,112 at Dallas. Mechanical faults, valve failures, and motor overheating accounted for nearly half of Atlanta's total.

Operator error tracking: The Afternoon Shift consistently recorded the highest operator error counts in both Georgia and Pennsylvania plants.

Georgia showed a flat error distribution across all shifts, suggesting a process design issue rather than a shift-specific one. Pennsylvania showed a sharper spike on the Afternoon Shift.

Line-level failure analysis: LINE5 in Atlanta and LINE1 in Philadelphia each recorded 82 failures (the highest at their respective facilities).
The assistant also identified that Philadelphia's top two lines accounted for 44% of its total failures.
 
Functional location downtime: Filler stations (FILLER01 nodes) dominated the top three downtime locations at both Atlanta and Dallas.

LINE2-FILLER01 in Atlanta accumulated 697.3 hours of downtime with 1,374 events, making it the single biggest reliability concern across both facilities.
 
Valve failure by equipment category: Across Atlanta, Dallas, and Los Angeles, the palletizer had the highest combined valve failure count (70), followed by the labeler (66).

Each facility had a different leading category, which means a single-site fix would miss the broader picture.
 
Why this matters
None of these questions are new. Maintenance supervisors, planners, and plant managers ask them regularly. The difference is speed and context.
With a custom AI agent, these questions get answered in seconds, grounded in live S/4HANA data. The agent connects to the system through MCP, which is SAP's open protocol for letting AI agents discover and call business APIs in a governed way. That means the answers come from the same source of truth that runs the maintenance processes.
SAP's direction here is clear. Joule Agents are purpose-built to execute multistep tasks across SAP and non-SAP systems. Joule Assistants coordinate those agents using role and process context. And Joule Studio provides the environment for building custom agents when prebuilt ones do not cover a specific need. This custom Asset Health Assistant is an example of that extensibility in action.
For asset management specifically, SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition already supports maintenance notification and order creation through Joule. The roadmap also includes agentic maintenance request initiation and screening as upcoming capabilities. The custom assistant we explored here goes further by combining failure analysis, OEE tracking, work order monitoring, and maintenance plan review into a single conversational experience.
 
What this means for asset-intensive operations
The value of this kind of assistant is practical. A plant manager preparing for a weekly review can ask for the top failure categories, check open work orders, and compare OEE across shifts in a few minutes. A maintenance planner can review condition-based plans, identify overdue orders, and spot patterns across facilities without leaving the conversation.
It also changes how teams collaborate around data. Instead of building a report and sending it to colleagues, a maintenance supervisor can walk through the same set of questions with the assistant during a meeting. Everyone sees the same data in real time.
This is not about replacing the expertise of maintenance teams. It is about removing the friction between a question and its answer. The knowledge sits in the system. The agent makes it accessible.
Looking ahead
SAP continues to expand what Joule can do inside S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. With MCP and A2A (Agent-to-Agent protocol) becoming standard, the ability to connect custom agents to SAP's business processes will only get easier. For asset management, that means moving from isolated dashboards to conversational, context-aware interactions that sit inside the flow of work.
If you are running asset-intensive operations on SAP Cloud ERP, building a custom assistant like this is worth exploring. The data is already there. The platform is ready. The question is whether your teams can get to the answers fast enough.

entry.title: Before the First Prompt: How SAP Engineers Trust Before Agents Are Ever Invoked
entry.content:
As enterprise AI evolves from conversational assistants to agentic systems capable of retrieving enterprise information, invoking tools, and initiating business workflows, the security challenge extends beyond protecting models and prompts. It requires governing the identities, permissions, data flows, integrations, and actions that connect AI to enterprise systems.

Trust must be engineered through clearly defined security boundaries, enforceable authorization controls, data protection measures, and accountable execution paths.

The SAP Business AI Platform is architected with exactly this in mind.

The SAP Agentic AI Ecosystem

This is the first blog in a three-part series on the security and governance of the SAP Agentic AI ecosystem. This post covers the trust foundation: how SAP builds and validates agents before they reach your landscape, how they are provisioned, and how identity, authorization, and data isolation are enforced. Part two “ Use Existing Agents, Build New Ones, Connect to Others — All Securely with SAP Joule Work”  covers the practitioner layer — using SAP agents, building custom extensions, and bridging third-party AI systems. Part three “The Agentic Glass Box: Observability and Governance at Enterprise Scale”concludes the series with the governance and observability architecture that gives enterprise teams the visibility and control to run AI at scale with confidence.

This post examines the first layer of that architecture — the controls SAP puts in place before a user sends a single message. It covers how security responsibilities are distributed across the agent supply chain, the provisioning model, and the identity and data isolation infrastructure; where those controls are enforced; and what enterprise IT leaders and CISOs should understand about the trust boundaries that govern agentic AI in SAP.

How SAP Ensures Agents Are Secure and Trustworthy Before You Provision Them

Every agent that appears in your SAP product catalog has passed through a structured security and governance program, built on a rigorous Secure Software Development and Operations Lifecycle, before it ever reaches your landscape. This program is built around the principle that trust must be earned through verifiable processes.

The foundation is controlled ownership and traceability. Each agent is formally registered within SAP with a defined owner, a declared scope, and a stable identity. It goes through multi-team review before it is eligible for customer deployment, and a complete Software Bill of Materials is generated automatically — documenting every component and dependency in the agent, giving a transparent view of what is running.

Security and governance are validated at every stage of development:

  • Every agent goes through a formal Ethics evaluation to verify fairness, transparency, human oversight (e.g., through human-in-the-loop) and alignment with global data privacy laws before development begins.
  • Agents go through a rigorous threat evaluation exercise performed to identify and mitigate risks during the design phase.
  • Code security is checked through mandatory automated scans covering application vulnerabilities, exposed credentials, and known weaknesses in third-party libraries, before the agent advances toward production
  • Authorization is managed as policy - agent-to-API permissions (e.g. read on a specific S/4 API resource) are assigned automatically during tenant mapping and provisioned as authorization policies in SAP Cloud Identity Services.
  • Audit logging is non-negotiable — every agent must implement security event logging.
  • All AI model interactions are routed through SAP AI Core — ensuring data residency, content filtering, and prompt injection protection can be enforced consistently, depending on the risk profile of the Agent.

Deployment follows a controlled, staged release process across development, test, and pre-production environments. Each step toward production requires an explicit human decision — there is no automated approval path from development to your landscape. The artifact that was validated in testing is the exact same artifact that reaches production; nothing is rebuilt or changed along the way.

Finally, every agent undergoes a formal security review before production release. The shared infrastructure SAP manages on your behalf — identity, network security, tenant isolation, geo-blocking — is covered automatically. The security review validates the agent's own logic, access controls, and AI-specific risks on top of the baseline.

By the time you see an agent in your SAP product catalog, it carries a documented chain of custody: who built it, what it contains, what security gates it passed, and what authorization model it enforces.

SAP for Me: Your Unified Hub for Subscription and Automated Provisioning

The lifecycle of an enterprise agent is governed by SAP for Me, which serves as the centralized control plane for provisioning and subscription management. This interface streamlines the deployment of Joule components, replacing complex manual BTP formations with a guided "Start Provisioning" workflow.

  • Governed Activation & Licensing: Customers activate specific agent scenarios (e.g., Finance Assistant, HR Service Desk) directly through SAP for Me. Access is strictly gated by valid subscription licenses (such as Joule-based or Early Adopter Care SKUs) and landscape prerequisites (e.g., connected S/4HANA or SuccessFactors systems). This ensures that only licensed, technically compatible agents are deployed within the enterprise topology.
  • Managed Orchestration & Trust: Under the SAP Managed Joule model, SAP assumes responsibility for the underlying infrastructure, including the Agent Gateway Formation. This mandatory formation establishes the secure, Service Provider Integration Interface (SPII) - based trust foundation (via IAS-backed destinations and token exchange) required for agent-to-agent communication. SAP manages the continuous updates, patching, and operational health of this global trust infrastructure, freeing customers from managing core AI runtime security.
  • Principal Propagation & Boundary Enforcement: Activation initiates the automated creation of service formations within the designated BTP subaccount. Security boundaries are enforced through principal propagation, where the Agent Gateway ensures that agent actions strictly respect the end-user's existing roles and identity context. This guarantees that agents operate only on data accessible to the user, preventing cross-tenant leakage or privilege escalation across integrated solutions.

 Example: Enabling Joule and AI Features in SAP SuccessFactors

By automating the technical "plumbing" in the background, SAP4Me allows you to maintain control over your high-level service settings while simplifying the onboarding experience.

The Identity & Authorization Framework (IAM) for SAP Agentic AI

 SAP Joule utilizes a robust governance model where AI agents are treated as first-class citizens—distinct service principals with their own boundaries and permissions. This architecture is built on SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS), which serves as the trust anchor and sole token issuer for agent identities.

To understand how this secures your data, we must look at the four distinct validation layers defined in the architecture:

 1. End user Authentication

End-users authenticate via standard enterprise protocols (OIDC/SAML) through SAP Cloud Identity Services. 

2. Validating User-to-Agent Access (Connectivity Governance)

The First Line of Defence. Before an agent even begins to work, the system must answer: "Is this user allowed to talk to this specific agent?"

  • How it works: When a user invokes Joule, the request is routed through the Agent Gateway which acts as the enforced single entry point for connectivity.
  • The Mechanism: Two layers work together
    • System connectivity is established through a UCL (Unified Customer Landscape) formation, which onboards the tenants/systems and wires up the trust (IAS App2App dependencies) between them. If that connection hasn't been formed, the caller can't even obtain a valid token to reach the agent.
    • User authorization is then checked against AMS (Authorization Management Service) policies — this is the per-user "is this user permitted to invoke this agent?" decision. (Agent and tool metadata itself lives in BTP, which is what the Gateway resolves the target against.).

A caller that is not connected and authorized is rejected before reaching the agent.

 3. Validating Agent-to-Tool Access (Orchestration Governance)

The Handshake. Once a user connects to an agent, the system must answer: "Is this agent allowed to use this tool?"

  • How it works: The Agent Gateway acts as a transparent proxy in front of tools and other agents. When an agent needs to execute a task, it presents its own IAS-issued, certificate-bound token; the Gateway performs the token exchange and injects the right credentials toward the target service.
  • The Mechanism: The Agent Gateway enforces authorization policies via AMS, checking whether a specific agent is allowed to call a specific tool (this is done with IAS token validation, mTLS, and tenant-mapping checks). This keeps every agent inside its defined scope — e.g., an HR agent can reach its HR systems but can't invoke a Finance tool it was never granted.

4. Validating Data Access (Functional Authorization)

The Final Security Layer. Finally, the system must answer: "Is this request allowed to see/read/write this specific data?"

  • How it works: The target application (e.g., SAP S/4HANA) enforces standard SAP Cloud Application authorization.
  • The Mechanism: This relies on established SAP concepts of Roles, Roles Catalogs, and Scopes. The agent's token includes the context of the original user. Therefore, the target application ensures that the action is only performed if the human user has permission to see that data (Row-Level Security).

This multi-layered approach ensures that governance is not a single point of failure. The system fails early: if the user lacks connectivity, the agent is never called; if the agent lacks functional authorization, the data is never touched.

 Data Segregation & Isolation

 A core tenet of Joule security is strict tenant isolation at every layer of the stack:

Your business data remains strictly isolated within your specific Line of Business applications, governed by the proven, multi-tenant security architecture already established in the backend systems. Access to this data is governed by the existing application logic, ensuring that even AI interaction is strictly constrained by functional or business rules supported by authorization.

 Metadata within the SAP Knowledge Graph and data in SAP HANA Cloud Vector Engine is strictly partitioned per Tenant. Joule leverages the SAP BTP multi-tenancy infrastructure to ensure that every query is bound to a specific tenant context. This ensures that there is no cross-tenant data leakage or overlap.

Joule utilizes Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to access enterprise data through the Generative AI Hub in SAP AI Core. Crucially, this process is automated and governed by strict multi-tenant isolation:

  • Automated Onboarding: You do not manually manage files or keys. Instead, you define "Grounding Sources" in the Generative AI Hub, pointing it to your backend systems (e.g., S/4HANA CDS Views, SAP Build Work Zone) via generic secrets. The platform automatically extracts metadata and ingests the content securely.
  • Tenant-Safe Vectorization: For unstructured data like PDFs or documents, the system processes the text and converts it into numerical vectors (embeddings). These are stored in the SAP HANA Cloud Vector Engine, where every piece of data is partitioned by your unique tenant identifier.
  • Architectural Isolation: Data separation is enforced at the infrastructure level through the platform's multi-tenancy model, which scopes every query to the caller's tenant context. This ensures that Joule can never retrieve or process data from another tenant.

Your prompts to Joule and the retrieved or processed data in Joule Work is not shared with third-party LLM providers for the purpose of training or improving their models. Your data is only sent to the LLM provider for processing and is not stored or otherwise retained by the LLM providers.

 

To Be Continued…

The controls described here are what make agentic AI deployable with confidence. But a secure foundation only matters if what you build on top of it holds up. Part two “ Use Existing Agents, Build New Ones, Connect to Others — All Securely with SAP Joule Work”  covers exactly that.
