entry.title: Use Existing Agents, Build New Ones, Connect to Others — All Securely with SAP Joule Work
entry.content:
Building a secure AI platform is a solved problem if you never let anyone use it. The hard part is maintaining that security posture when real users are invoking agents through Conversations and Spaces, developers are extending the platform with custom workflows and code-based capabilities, and integration teams are connecting Joule Work to the broader AI ecosystem the enterprise already runs.

Each of these activities expands the security perimeter. Each introduces new integration points, new identity flows, and new data pathways. Governed well, they amplify what the platform can do. Left unstructured, they introduce exactly the kind of fragmentation that erodes the trust the foundation was designed to establish.

This is the second post in a three-part series on the security and governance of the SAP Agentic AI ecosystem. Part one ”Before the First Prompt: How SAP Engineers Trust Before Agents Are Ever Invoked” covered the trust foundation — how SAP builds and validates agents, how they are provisioned, and how identity and data isolation are enforced before a user ever interacts with the platform. This post covers what happens when you put that platform to work: using SAP's existing agents, building your own, and connecting to third-party systems and tools. Part three “The Agentic Glass Box: Observability and Governance at Enterprise Scale” concludes the series with the governance and observability architecture that gives enterprise teams the visibility and control to run AI at scale with confidence.

This post covers three areas where the tension between extensibility and security plays out in practice. First, how users engage with Joule Work's first two core surfaces — Conversations and Spaces — and the governance model that keeps every interaction authenticated, identity-bound, and traceable. Second area focuses on Joule work’s third core surface, Develop, which deals with how developers extend the platform securely — through Joule Studio's low-code environment, the agent extensibility skills engine, and the Bring Your Own Agent path — without compromising the security architecture established in Part one. Third, how SAP governs the boundary between Joule Work and the rest of your AI landscape, namely, inbound access from third-party agents, and outbound connectivity to external MCP servers and data sources.

 

The Three Pillars of Joule Work: Designed for Productivity, Built for Trust

Conversations: Intent-Driven Work with Governed Execution

Conversations is where users express what they need in plain language, and Joule's orchestration translates intent into actionable outcomes or precise answers through a grounding, planning, and execution loop. At runtime, Joule securely invokes deployed agents based on contextual routing rules, BTP service bindings, and governance policies, the calls are brokered centrally through the Agent Gateway, which authenticates and authorizes each call ensuring every agent call is authenticated, encrypted, and restricted to integrations and deployment environments a customer has approved.

For knowledge-based queries, Joule uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to ground responses in verified enterprise knowledge (SAP Help or customer documents) and real-time system context, and connected data sources, reducing inaccuracies while keeping the reasoning traceable. When accessing data or calling APIs, Joule operates under the initiating user's authorization context. Identity is propagated through the Agent Gateway using IAS-issued tokens and token exchange, so backend calls respect the user's existing roles and permissions (principal propagation).

Agent interactions are observable and logged. The Agent Gateway records agent calls, and Joule Work's governed execution contexts add source attribution and an audit trail around agentic work — giving organizations a traceable record of which agents were engaged and on whose behalf data was accessed.

 

Spaces: Dynamic Context with Strict Governance

Spaces: dynamically assemble the data, insights, agents, and actions relevant to a specific task into a single real-time workspace — composed on demand for the work at hand. Beyond productivity, Spaces function within strict security boundaries.

Work performed inside a Space adheres to Joule Work’s governed orchestration and identity model: agents execute strictly within the user's authorization context, ensuring all actions are authenticated on the user's behalf. Access to the workspace is governed by app-managed space permissions (Ex: owner, editor, reader), which define granular control per Space.

Joule enforces strict security boundaries by scoping all data access and agent execution to a specific spaceId and userId mapping, preventing cross-workspace leakage. Additionally, Space data is partitioned per tenant at the infrastructure level. Every human decision and AI action generates structured telemetry events, creating a comprehensive, auditable workflow chain for enterprise governance.

 

Develop: Extensibility Built on a Secure Foundation

Develop is the unified entry point for organizations to build custom agents, workflows, and applications that extend Joule to unique business processes. It empowers both professional developers via code and citizen engineers via low-code tools, all within a governed environment.

Joule Work supports two distinct types of extensibility: Low-Code automation via managed n8n and extending Code-Based agents via the Agent Extensibility Engine

Managed Low-Code Orchestration (n8n)

For process-driven tasks, Joule provides a fully managed n8n environment embedded directly into the SAP Business AI Platform via Joule Studio. This gives business technologists and developers a visual interface to design complex multi-agent workflows using hundreds of pre-built native connectors plus universal HTTP/REST nodes—allowing businesses to bridge their SAP systems to external SaaS tools in minutes.

  • Infrastructure & Compliance: n8n runs on SAP's managed cloud infrastructure, it operates as a fully embedded, multi-tenant SaaS experience on SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP). It is provisioned under strict tenant isolation boundaries—each customer receives dedicated database storage and unique service bindings for resources like AI Core—ensuring that data remains within the customer’s designated trust perimeter. This architecture supports enterprise requirements for multi-tenancy, lifecycle management, and regional availability while maintaining GDPR compliance through SAP's managed infrastructure controls.
  • Secure Access (The "How"): The instance is protected by a dedicated per-tenant proxy API. This proxy acts as the sole entry point, ensuring all executions are authenticated and tenant-isolated before they ever touch internal logic.
  • Credential & Egress Management: Secrets are encrypted in an enterprise credential vault. Additionally, network egress rules enforce strict boundaries to ensure data does not flow to unauthorized external domains.
  • Identity Integration: Managed n8n integrates directly with enterprise identity services (IAS) at runtime, ensuring that workflow metadata and service accounts resolve against existing organizational policies.

Example : Creating n8n Workflows in Joule Studio

Extending Code-Based Agent 

Professional developers build complex capabilities as Skills using the Agent Extensibility Engine. These are reusable modules containing custom logic that agents can consume.

  • Dynamic Capability Loading: Skills (containing Tools, Instructions, and Hooks) are stored in the User Metadata Service (UMS) on BTP and fetched dynamically at runtime via the App Foundation SDK.
  • Implicit Boundary Enforcement: This separation ensures an agent can only access extensions explicitly defined for its capability ID, preventing "privilege creep" or unauthorized API interactions that static bundling might allow.

Example: Use Joule Studio to Extend the AP Invoice Agent using Agent Extensions

 

To bridge the gap between standard platform capabilities and specialized operational requirements, you might need to develop custom agents tailored to your specific business use cases.  For this purpose and to accommodate varying technical expertise in your work force, Joule Work provides two distinct pathways: a guided, low-code experience in Joule Studio for citizen developers, and an open 'Bring Your Own Agent' model for professional engineers. Both approaches leverage the platform’s enterprise-grade security, governance, and runtime infrastructure to ensure secure, production-ready deployments:

 Build your own agent using Joule studio.

If you prefer visual tools and low/no code, Joule Studio provides a web-based Agent Builder. This environment enables intent-driven development—allowing you to define capabilities in plain language while the platform generates the underlying artifacts.

Step-by-Step Workflow

  1. Define Intent: Enter a natural language description of your use case. Joule Studio automatically generates a Product Requirements Document (PRD), identifying user personas and expected outcomes.
  2. Configure & Connect: Name the agent, set behavioural instructions, and extend its capabilities by connecting to:
    • Data Sources: SAP Destinations (S/4HANA, SuccessFactors) or third-party APIs.
    • Tools: MCP servers for external tooling integration.
    • Logic: Existing Joule Skills or n8n workflows.
  3. Model Selection: Choose from the available catalog of LLMs managed via SAP AI Core. All models are pre-benchmarked for performance and safety.
  4. Test & Deploy: Validate the agent using Joule Studio’s built-in "Playground" to simulate conversations and edge cases. Deployment triggers a governed CI/CD pipeline; however, agents require manual human approval before promotion and activation in production.
  5. Authenticate & Secure Tool Calls: Once deployed, Agent-to-tool and agent-to-agent communications are routed through the Agent Gateway, which serves as the central ingress point handling request validation, traffic distribution, and rate limiting. Authentication between services is managed via SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS) App2App tokens, ensuring that agents only communicate with authorized destinations while maintaining secure session lifecycles across the platform.

Example: Build a Supplier Performance Assistant Agent with Joule Studio and SAP S/4HANA Cloud

Bring Your Own Agent – and let it work with Joule

“Bring Your Own Agent”, as Pro-code agents option in Joule Work offer developers full control over reasoning, state management, and custom system integration. These agents are developed in independent environments and connected to Joule Work via open standards.

Step-by-Step Workflow

1. Local Development & Framework Selection: Developers use the Joule Studio CLI alongside standard IDEs (e.g., VS Code) for validation, packaging, and deployment. You build agent logic using your preferred open-source frameworks—such as LangGraph/LangChain for stateful reasoning, CrewAI/AG2 for multi-agent collaboration, or Google ADK—and leverage standard SAP BTP SDKs to handle AI Core model calls, destination management, and telemetry.

2. Mandatory Security Contracts (SPII): Before the agent can be registered, it must implement specific integration handlers—hard gates that ensure secure tenant mapping:

  • Tenant Mapping Endpoint: A mandatory PATCH /v1/tenantMappings/{tenantId} handler to manage subscription lifecycles and receive tenant-scoped configuration waves.
  • Audit Logging: Integration with the platform's audit logging service to track security-relevant events from the moment of subscription.

   3. Deployment Runtime Options: You can deploy your agent to one of two runtimes:

  • Option A — SAP Managed Runtime (App Foundation): Deployed via a governed CI/CD pipeline onto Kyma (BTP). This should follow a staged promotion ladder (Development Landscape → Quality Assurance Landscape→ Pre-Production Landscape → Production Landscape), requiring manual approvals and automatically provisioning observability, tenant isolation, and regional routing.
  • Option B — Customer-Managed BTP Subaccount: The agent runs entirely in the customer's own subaccount, giving them full infrastructure control while still connecting to Joule via standard protocols.

 4. A2A Endpoint Exposure & Discovery: To integrate with Joule Work, the deployed agent must expose a standardized Agent-to-Agent (A2A) server endpoint and register its capabilities:

  • Open Resource Discovery (ORD): An ORD document registers the agent's metadata in the Unified Metadata Service (UMS), making it discoverable across the platform.
  • A2A Capabilities: The agent exposes an Agent Card (describing name, tasks, and capabilities like streaming) and a task processing endpoint where Joule can send and receive requests.

5. Registration & Invocation in Joule Work: Finally, the agent is registered within Joule by creating a Joule Scenario with a Dialog Function (action type agent-request) pointing to your A2A endpoint. Authentication is secured via IAS App2App tokens—validating issuer, audience, and scope on every request. Once registered, users can invoke the agent directly through Joule Work's conversational interface, and Joule's orchestration engine will automatically route the intent to your custom capability.

Example: Building a Pro-Code Agent on SAP BTP

Architecture : Custom Pro-Code AI Agents on SAP BTP

By combining the flexibility of extension tools with the rigor of extensibility governance, organizations can innovate rapidly without compromising the security posture required for enterprise operations.

SAP is deepening its technical collaboration with NVIDIA to embed OpenShell — an open-source, secure runtime for AI agents — directly into the Joule Studio runtime on SAP Business AI Platform. OpenShell provides isolated execution environments, filesystem and network policy enforcement, and runtime-level containment for agents, operating on the principle that security lives in the environment, not in the model or application layer. Nothing is permitted by default — permissions are granted based on policies enforced outside the agent itself. This collaboration is working toward making every agent deployed through Joule Studio inspectable, governable, and auditable by design, with a roadmap that includes regulated-industry readiness across FedRAMP and FIPS standards.

Secure Bridging of SAP and Third-Party Services

1.    Inbound Connectivity: Third-Party Agents Securely Accessing SAP

Enterprises often utilize partner AI ecosystems (like Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock, etc.) as front-end interaction layers. These external platforms need to invoke deep SAP business capabilities—such as triggering an Autonomous Finance agent or querying a Joule Skill—without building fragile point-to-point integrations.

How It Works: We enforce a "One Governed Door" architecture. Every inbound request from a third-party agent is routed exclusively through the Agent Gateway (AGW). There is absolutely no direct network access to SAP business systems. The connectivity relies on the open-standard Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, ensuring seamless interoperability across platform boundaries without custom code for each partner.

Governance & Security:

  • Onboarding: A customer’s IT admin onboards the third-party agent via SAP4Me and Unified Customer Landscape (UCL). This triggers a secure formation pipeline that provisions a dedicated, tenant-scoped OIDC identity in SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS/SCI).. 
  • Strict Authentication: Integration utilizes mTLS (Mutual TLS) for infrastructure-level trust and standard OAuth2/OIDC token exchange at runtime. Every inbound request presents credentials scoped specifically to that customer’s tenant, validated against a trusted SAP PKI allowlist.
  • Customer-Gated Access Control: Governance is enforced by the Agent Gateway. It acts as an intelligent allowlist, ensuring a third-party agent can only invoke the specific SAP agents the customer explicitly approved. No unauthorized or unlisted capabilities are exposed.
  • Identity Preservation: The acting user’s identity is propagated end-to-end. Even if the call originates from an external partner UI, the underlying SAP execution respects the original user's authorizations and data boundaries.

2.    Integration: Connecting Customers to External MCP Servers

The Scenario: Customers need Joule to access rich, real-time data from external environments—such as custom cloud repositories, public API marketplaces, or on-premise systems. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables this by allowing Joule Work and Joule Studio to dynamically discover and utilize these external tools as native extensions.

How It Works: Joule leverages the BTP Destination Service to resolve connection configurations.

  • For internet-based MCP servers, the runtime resolves the destination tag (mcp=true) and initiates direct HTTPS calls after authentication resolution.
  • For on-premise targets, connectivity is securely bridged via the BTP Connectivity Service and the customer’s established Cloud Connector tunnel, ensuring traffic never touches public endpoints.

Governance & Security:

  • Scoped Token Exchange (Zero Raw JWT Leakage): To prevent over-privileged access, Joule rejects sending raw user JWTs to external MCP servers. Instead, it performs an OAuth User Token Exchange, issuing a narrowly-scoped, short-lived token specific only to the target MCP server’s entitlements. This ensures the external server cannot see the user's full enterprise BTP access surface.
  • Tenant Isolation: External calls are brokered through the Agent Gateway / Unified Outbound Gateway, which maintains tenant isolation and applies authorization before a request leaves the secure boundary.
  • Auditability & Visibility: Every extension deployment and execution is logged via telemetry dashboards. Admins have full visibility into which external MCP servers are connected, who authorized them.

To Be Continued…

Each capability described in this post — using agents, extending the platform, connecting to third parties — expands the security perimeter. The Joule Work architecture is designed so the controls move with it.

What remains is to be confident that everything described here is working as intended, continuously, at scale. That is where the final post “The Agentic Glass Box: Observability and Governance at Enterprise Scale” comes in.

entry.title: The Agentic Glass Box: Observability and Governance at Enterprise Scale
entry.content:
Knowing that an agent was built securely and knowing that it is behaving securely right now are two different things. The trust foundation that Part one described — vetted supply chains, governed provisioning, enforced identity — is a starting point, not a guarantee. Agents evolve. Configurations change. New integrations are added. The ecosystem grows. And as it grows, the need for visibility becomes not a nice-to-have but a hard governance requirement.

Enterprise AI cannot operate as a black box. Not for regulators. Not for auditors. Not for the IT and security teams responsible for what happens when an agent makes the wrong call at scale. The answer is a glass box approach: every agent action observable, every identity traceable, every data access auditable — not eventually, but by design, from the moment an agent is deployed.

This is the third and final post in the series. Part one ”Before the First Prompt: How SAP Engineers Trust Before Agents Are Ever Invoked” built the trust foundation. Part two “ Use Existing Agents, Build New Ones, Connect to Others — All Securely with SAP Joule Work”  covered using, extending, and connecting agents. This post closes the loop — the governance and observability layer that gives enterprise teams real-time visibility, cross-platform control, and compliance-grade audit trails across the entire Joule Work ecosystem.

It covers three areas: how Joule Work's security model adapts across Web, Mobile, and Desktop; how the SAP AI Agent Hub in SAP LeanIX acts as a vendor-agnostic command centre for governing every AI asset in your landscape; and how the monitoring and audit architecture — built on OpenTelemetry, the SAP Audit Log Service, and integrated with Cloud ALM and Signavio — delivers the traceability enterprise governance demands.

 Governance Across Modalities

Joule adapts its security posture to the device context: Web, Mobile, and Desktop.

Joule Work Web

Joule Work Web is the core AI workspace running in the browser with a platform-first security model focused on tenant isolation, identity-bound access, and governed agent execution.

  • Identity: Access is gated by SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) Identity Authentication Service (IAS) by assigning users to the joule_end_user group.
  • Session Management: Uses token-based session management with short expiration times.
  • Network Security: All communication occurs over secure TLS.
  • Data access: Joule responses only surface data the authenticated user is already authorized to see
  • Tenant-level data isolation : Customer data stays within the customer's own SAP tenancy; no customer data is stored within Joule itself

Joule Work Mobile App

Joule Work Mobile brings Joule to the enterprise edge — iOS, Android, and wearables — with a security model anchored in device governance, MDM-enforced access policies, and full data erasure on offboarding

  • SSO via short-lived tokens, with SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS) as the primary IdP — supports proxy to corporate IdPs (e.g. Microsoft Entra ID)
  • Configurable Remember Me session cookies when IAS is active
  • MDM integration enables automated onboarding, conditional access, and app protection policies
  • Remote wipe and inactivity-based auto-deregistration remove access and data on lost or inactive devices
  • Local data encrypted with AES-256 (iOS additionally uses Keychain); all traffic over HTTPS
  • Sign-out permanently removes all personal data and configurations from the device
  • Access to security settings, feature flags, and user management is gated by a dedicated MobileAdmin BTP Role Collection
  • Enterprise app distribution requires signed builds (Apple certificates/provisioning profiles); admin-configurable support log uploads for audit and troubleshooting

Refer: Joule Work Mobile App – Administration Guide

Joule Work Desktop

Joule Work Desktop extends AI capabilities to local files (PDFs, Code, Office docs) with a unique security model focused on data privacy:

  • Users must be explicitly assigned — no self-service enrolment. Authentication and Authorizations is managed by SAP IAS
  • User conversations remain locally stored on user device, user can delete at any time.
  • The Desktop extension acts as a sandboxed process. It cannot access the operating system's clipboard or other application memory without specific, user-initiated actions.
  • Governance of which MCPs the user can use, happens via the Admin UI. In the Admin UI, customer admins can define allow/blocklists for certain MCPs. These settings are fetched by the client and enforced on client side. User can only enable those MCP servers on the client which are allowed.

 

Vendor-agnostic command center - SAP AI Agent Hub

 

SAP AI Agent Hub: Your command center for AI governance

AI Agent Hub works in conjecture with already existing SAP products (Ex: Cloud ALM, Signavio, SuccessFactors) to enhance the experience of building an agent, monitoring of the process and agent health and workforce impact. We will discuss these capabilities below.

 

Architecture Decisions Inventory

 By integrating SAP LeanIX’s context-rich enterprise architecture inventory with the AI Agent Hub, organizations embed governance directly into the agent development lifecycle. The Architecture Decisions view captures foundational technical and policy choices (e.g., LLM framework selection, PII data handling strategies, initial scaling limits) and automatically surfaces these guardrails during agent creation. This ensures new agents are aligned with established architectural standards from day one rather than requiring retrospective remediation.

Real-Time Landscape Discovery & Dependency Mapping

During development, the integrated MCP server continuously queries the live LeanIX landscape to perform automated capability mapping and dependency analysis. As the agent builder progresses through business understanding, fit-gap assessment, and process design, it automatically:

  • Identifies relevant existing agents (e.g., Invoice Mapper Agent)
  • Surfaces supporting applications & data sources (e.g., S/4HANA Private Cloud, Oracle, custom SAP systems)
  • Maps cross-system dependencies and process touchpoints

This eliminates manual landscape research and ensures agents are grounded in the actual enterprise architecture, preventing duplicate investments and unplanned integration risks.

 

AI Agent Discovery Inbox

SAP AI Agent Hub — a capability within SAP LeanIX — has the AI Agent Discovery Inbox which provides centralized visibility into all AI artifacts across the enterprise—agents, MCP servers, and LLM instances—regardless of origin or vendor. Integrated usage analytics (activation history, session volume, trend patterns) enable governance teams to prioritize high-impact interventions. Discovered assets enter a unified workflow for rapid assessment, classification, and inventory onboarding.

 

Verification Workflow & Compliance Enforcement

Unlike traditional platforms that treat agents as isolated IT components, SAP AI Agent Hub maps each agent as a first-class enterprise architecture artifact. Every agent is explicitly linked to:

  • The business capability it enables
  • Downstream applications and data flows it depends on
  • The value stream/processes it participates in

The Verification Workflow subject all inventory entries to structured assessment against organizational risk criteria, compliance mandates, and architecture standards. Successful verification generates a formal audit trail capturing approval authority, ownership, operational scope, and dependency impact. Only verified agents are permitted in production, effectively closing the approve-to-run gap and standardizing governance expectations across development teams.

 

Agent Operation Overview

Agent Mining in SAP Signavio applies process mining algorithms to agent execution traces, reconstructing how agents actually behave in production. It produces a discovered execution model showing every path taken, path frequency, and deviations from the intended design — going beyond session-level observability to surface the full range of execution variants, including edge cases.

Agent Performance Deep Drive

The view above in SAP Signavio Agent Mining translates the mined execution model into prioritized optimization opportunities, functioning as a closed-loop business-outcome feedback mechanism. By connecting behavioral patterns directly to measurable KPIs, it quantifies return on investment and surfaces actionable insights. When agents follow incorrect execution paths at high frequency, it signals a systematic misalignment between agent design and business intent—not merely an isolated failure. Optimization potential is evaluated not only on technical metrics but on actual process outcomes: is the workflow the agent was deployed to improve actually performing better? This closes the gap between agent deployment and tangible value realization, enabling organizations to focus efforts on their most effective agents—answering the ROI and performance questions that leadership increasingly demands but few can currently provide.

 

AI Agent Monitoring in SAP Cloud ALM provides two levels of visibility into agent health and behaviour across the enterprise.

Deep Dive View

Session-Level Visibility (Deep Dive): Traces a single execution of the agent in detail—covering latency, token usage, and tool invocation flows. By utilizing underlying OpenTelemetry traces, engineers can reproduce issues, inspect reasoning steps, and understand exactly how the agent interacted with backend systems like S/4HANA. Every session is logged to ensure compliance-grade auditability.

High-Level View

Portfolio-Level Overview (High-Level): Displays the aggregate health of an agent across the environment using real-time dashboards. Key metrics such as Goal Completion Rate and Total Call Accuracy trend over time, allowing teams to quickly distinguish between isolated incidents and systemic issues. If an anomaly is detected, the dashboard provides a root-cause breakdown of the risk category (e.g., usage spikes or accuracy drops), enabling rapid response and data-driven governance decisions.

 

SAP SucessFactors Integration

SAP SuccessFactors helps you understand how your agent deployment strategy is reshaping your workforce. Each agent is mapped to the business units and roles it affects, giving HR and business leaders visibility into which skills are impacted, which teams are using agents, and how the workforce is changing as AI deployment scales.

Together, these integrations span the full agent governance lifecycle. SAP LeanIX grounds every agent in the enterprise architecture — ensuring it is aligned to established standards. SAP AI Agent Hub discovers the agents, the agents can be verified and enabled for production. SAP Signavio reveals how agents actually behave once deployed, surfacing deviations from intended design and connecting execution patterns to business outcomes. SAP Cloud ALM provides the operational layer — real-time health monitoring at both the session and portfolio level, with the depth engineers need to investigate and the breadth leadership needs to govern. SAP SuccessFactors closes the loop on the human side, mapping agent deployment to workforce and organizations. 

Observability and Compliance

Trust requires visibility. Joule provides a "Glass Box" architecture for enterprise monitoring:

  • Observability (OpenTelemetry): Agent runtimes are instrumented with OpenTelemetry — the standard SAP has adopted for logs, metrics, and traces — and Joule Studio's Traces & Explainability surface lets users inspect agent execution traces for transparency and debugging.
  • Audit logging (SAP Audit Log Service): Security-relevant events generated by agents and their interactions — such as authentications, authorization/validation errors, and unauthenticated access attempts — are recorded through the SAP Audit Log Service (the BTP audit log offering)
  • SIEM integration: Audit log events are forwarded from the SAP Audit Log Service to enterprise SIEM systems for further security analysis.
  • Content safety: Inputs and outputs can pass through AI Core Orchestration Service's content filtering, they scan for and block non-compliant content.
  • Runtime containment (NVIDIA OpenShell): SAP's collaboration with NVIDIA embeds OpenShell into the Joule Studio runtime, providing isolated execution boundaries, network and filesystem policy enforcement, and runtime-level auditability — ensuring agent actions are governed and inspectable at the environment level, independent of the model or application code.

Summary

This series has traced the governance challenge of enterprise agentic AI from its origin to its resolution. Part one established the trust foundation before agents are ever invoked — supply chain controls, provisioning governance, and identity architecture that ensure every agent starts from a verified baseline. Part two showed how that foundation holds under the pressure of real work: users engaging through Conversations and Spaces, developers extending the platform via Joule Studio and BYOA paths, and the enterprise bridging its SAP systems to third-party AI ecosystems — all within a "one governed door" architecture enforced by the Agent Gateway. This post closed the loop, demonstrating how Joule's security model adapts across Web, Mobile, and Desktop modalities; how the SAP AI Agent Hub provides a vendor-agnostic command center that maps every AI asset back to the business processes and risk criteria it touches; and how observability — through OpenTelemetry, the SAP Audit Log Service, SIEM integration, and NVIDIA OpenShell's runtime containment — transforms Joule Work into a glass box.

Note: this architecture is evolving — capabilities, integrations, and controls described here will continue to develop as the platform matures.

entry.title: When I ask Joule something, what actually happens behind the scenes?
entry.content:
At first glance it may feel like you are simply chatting with an AI assistant. In reality there is an intelligent orchestration layer working behind the scenes to ensure every response is accurate, secure and connected to your business systems. Let's break it down.

Step 1: Everything starts with the user - Every interaction begins with a person. There are two ways a user can interact with AI:

  • Through Joule by asking a question (for example, "Who hasn't completed their performance review?")
  • Directly inside SAP SuccessFactors (HCM) by clicking an action, such as approving leave or updating employee information. Both paths eventually lead to the same AI engine.

Step 2: Joule or HCM sends the request to the Agent Runtime - The Agent Runtime acts like the brain or orchestrator. Instead of immediately generating an answer, it first plans the best way to fulfil the request.

  • Its job is to understand the request and decide: What information is needed?, Which systems should be contacted?, Which tools should be used?, Is the user authorized to perform this action?

Step 3: Agent Configuration decides how the request should be handled - Inside the Agent Runtime are three important components.

  1. Agent Config - This is the AI's instruction manual. It defines: which agent should respond, what workflow to follow and which business rules apply.
  2. A2A Client (Agent-to-Agent) - Sometimes one AI agent cannot complete the task alone. t may need help from another specialized agent. It defines: one agent understands HR policies, another specializes in recruiting and another handles payroll.
  3. MCP Client - The MCP Client connects AI with enterprise systems. Instead of creating separate integrations for every application MCP provides one standard way to communicate with: SAP applications, databases, APIs, documents, custom enterprise systems

Step 4: Selecting the right tools - Once the runtime understands the request, it chooses the most suitable tool. The user never needs to choose these tools manually. Joule automatically selects the best one.

  • It might use: Calculator, Web Search, SAP Joule Functions, Custom enterprise applications, MCP-connected enterprise tools

Step 5: Large Language Models (LLM) do the reasoning - Once all the required information is collected, everything is sent to the Large Language Model (LLM). This is where AI actually thinks to generate an intelligent response.

  • The LLM combines: your question, enterprise data, tool outputs, business context,

Step 6: Agent Services keep everything secure - While all of this happens, another layer called Agent Services continuously monitors the process. It provides:

  • Guardrails – ensures AI follows company policies.
  • Metering – tracks resource usage.
  • Tracing – records what happened during each request.
  • Benchmarking – measures performance and quality.
  • Extensibility – allows organizations to add new capabilities in the future.

This architecture shows that Joule is much more than a chatbot. It acts as an intelligent coordinator that understands your request, connects to the right enterprise systems, collaborates with specialized AI agents, uses the appropriate tools, reasons with Large Language Models and delivers secure, governed and business-aware responses all within a unified AI framework.

  1. What data does SAP Knowledge Graph cover out of the box, and can it be extended with custom or non-SAP data?SAP Knowledge Graph is pre-modeled and available out of the box; no configuration is required to get started. Today, it contains reference information based on SAP's standard data model. However, SAP Knowledge Graph will soon extend to customer-specific metadata. Non-SAP data can also be onboarded into the SAP ecosystem via SAP Business Data Cloud, making it accessible to SAP Knowledge Graph as well.

There is no license nor additional cost for SAP Knowledge Graph (the use of Joule, Joule Studio or AI agents might generate costs).

    We hear both the curiosity and the desire to get closer to the data that's shaping your AI experiences. For now, we're intentionally keeping the underlying content protected, direct query access isn't something we're planning to offer. entry.title: 【EventPreview】SAP TechEd Berlin 2026：行く前にカタログを全部数えてみた／Counting Every Session Before I Go
entry.content:
（※English version is available in the latter half of this article.）

※免責事項

本稿は JSUG テクニカル部会のオピニオンリーダーとしての個人の見解であり、JSUG の公式な見解ではありません。セッションの集計と文章の一部には生成AIを使っています。内容の正確性は保証できませんので、情報の活用はご自身の判断でお願いします。

この記事のポイント

  • SAP TechEd Berlin 2026（308件）と ASUG Tech Connect 2026（176件）の公開セッションカタログを、参加前に全件数えてみました。
  • どちらも主役は AI エージェントです（セッションの4〜5割）。TechEd では、AI を「作る」トラックより「設計・運用・保護する」トラックのほうが大きく、全社の AI ガバナンスも独立したトラックになっています。
  • 5月の Sapphire で発表された Joule Work、SAP AI Agent Hub、Joule Studio などは、TechEd ではハンズオンや顧客の話として出てきます。一方で、Anthropic や NVIDIA の名前はカタログに出てきません。
  • ASUG は、移行・費用・ガバナンス・規制の比率が TechEd の2〜3倍です。TechEd は「移行を AI で速くする」、ASUG は「AI のために足元を整える」という向きで、SAP の Christian Klein 氏と ASUG の Geoff Scott 氏の最近の発言もそれぞれ同じ方向を指しています。
  • 現地で見てきたことは、12月8日の JSUG Conference と、1月に予定しているテクニカル部会でお届けします。

はじめに

10月27日から29日まで、ベルリンで SAP TechEd が開かれます。その1週間後、11月2日から4日には米国フォートワースで ASUG Tech Connect があります。JSUG テクニカル部会からは、今年も両方にメンバーが参加します。私はベルリンに行きます。

昨年は ASUG Tech Connect に参加したあとでレポートを書きました。今年は、行く前に書いてみることにしました。

きっかけは出発前の下調べです。どの回に出るかを決めようと公開のセッションカタログを眺めていたのですが、数が多くて目では追いきれません。そこで 、TechEd と ASUG Tech Connect のカタログを全件取得し、形式・トラック・キーワードで数えてみました。すると、一覧を眺めているだけでは気づかなかった傾向がいくつか見えてきました。

これから参加する方、オンラインで見る予定の方、今年は見送る方にも、全体をつかむ材料になればと思ってまとめておきます。数字はすべて10月6日時点の公開カタログによるものです。

1. おさらい：SAP のイベントの位置づけ

ご存じの方も多いと思いますが、簡単におさらいしておきます。SAP が自ら主催する大きなイベントは、今は次の3つです。

  • SAP Sapphire（5月）：経営と事業の発表。オーランド会場は ASUG の年次大会と合同です
  • SAP Connect（10月）：業務部門向け。人事・調達・財務などの大会を、2025年に1つにまとめたものです
  • SAP TechEd（10月）：IT と技術者向け

TechEd には地域版（TechEd on Tour）があり、北米では ASUG Tech Connect がその役割を担っています。日本向けには SAP ジャパンによるオンラインの SAP TechEd Japan があり、JSUG ではメンバーが現地に行って、JSUG Conference等 で報告しています。

2. 今年の流れ：5月に構想、10月に提供開始、そして技術の中身へ

今年の SAP は、5月の Sapphire で「自律型企業（Autonomous Enterprise）」と SAP Business AI Platform を打ち出しました。50以上のアシスタントと200以上のエージェントという構想が示されています。

10月上旬の SAP Connect では、その仕組みの一般提供が始まることが発表されました。ただし、個別のアシスタントの多くは2026年末から2027年初めにかけての提供予定です。

その流れで迎えるのが今回の TechEd です。経営向けに語られた構想が、技術者向けにはどういう中身として語られるのか。今年はそこを見る回だと思っています。

【📷 図1：fig1-event-flow.png／SAP's 2026 event flow from Sapphire to the JSUG Technical SIG】

 

 

3. Sapphire の発表は、TechEd でどう形になっているか

5月の Sapphire で発表されたものが TechEd でどう扱われているかを、カタログで追ってみました。発表の段階だったものが、ハンズオンや顧客の話として出てきています。

  • Joule Work：Sapphire で紹介された、Joule を中心にした新しい作業画面です。TechEd では25件のセッションに登場し、デスクトップ・モバイル・Web で動かすハンズオン（JW163・JW164・JW261）があります。JW206 では、製造・小売・企業 IT で本番運用している顧客の話が紹介されるようです。
  • SAP AI Agent Hub：Sapphire で「7〜9月に提供」とされたエージェントの台帳です。TechEd では、エージェントの発見から廃止までを試すハンズオン（BT161）と、SAP 自身が社内でどう使っているかの回（BT116）が並びます。
  • Joule Studio：51件と、いちばん多く登場します。自分でエージェントを作るハンズオンが複数あるほか、SAP Build から Joule Studio への移行の進め方（AD106）や、移行を準備している製造業 Knapp の話（ST126）もあります。
  • Joule のアシスタント：調達（AS264 Sourcing Assistant）や決算（AS260 Financial Closing Assistant）のアシスタントを実際に触れるハンズオンがあります。
  • SAP Business Data Cloud：データをコピーせずに共有するハンズオン（DA162）や、Henkel で SAP と Adobe のエージェントが連携する事例（DA206）があります。

一方で、Sapphire で大きく取り上げられた外部のパートナー、Anthropic（Claude）と NVIDIA の名前は、TechEd のカタログには一度も出てきません。Databricks も4件だけです。カタログに書かれていないだけで中身として扱われないとは限りませんが、TechEd では「SAP の製品として何ができるか」に話が集中しているように見えます。

4. TechEd Berlin 2026 のカタログを数えてみた

TechEd Berlin のセッションは308件あります。

まず感じたのは、主役がはっきりしていることです。タイトルか概要に AI エージェントが出てくるセッションは144件、全体の47%でした。製品名で多いのも SAP Business AI Platform、Joule、Joule Studio です。

意外だったのはトラックの構成です。9本あるトラックのうち最大は「Architect, operate, and secure AI at scale（AI の設計・運用・保護）」で57件。エージェントやアプリを「作る」トラック（49件）より多いのです。さらに「Drive AI governance for enterprise-wide impact（全社の AI ガバナンス）」が独立したトラックとして27件あります。中身を見ると、エージェントの台帳（SAP AI Agent Hub）、監視（SAP Cloud ALM）、SAP 自身の社内での運用事例などが並んでいます。AI を作る話から、作ったものをどう管理するかの話へ、重心が少しずつ移ってきているように見えます。

【📷 図2：fig2-teched-tracks.png／Sessions per track at SAP TechEd Berlin 2026】

 

一方で、気になった点もあります。

  • 規制（EU AI 法など）に触れるセッションはほとんどありません。ガバナンスは主に、台帳・監視・費用・廃止といった運用管理として語られています。
  • 登壇者の区分が付いた244件のうち232件が SAP です。TechEd のカタログは「SAP が何を打ち出しているか」の地図として読むのがよさそうです。

ちなみに、基盤の呼び名も変わりつつあります。TechEd のカタログでは「SAP Business AI Platform」が41件、「BTP」は1件だけでした。

5. ASUG Tech Connect と比べると

ASUG Tech Connect 2026 のセッションは176件です（公式には190以上とされ、毎週追加されています）。そのうち44件は TechEd と同じ題目の再演です。

主題が AI エージェントなのは同じです。違うのは、その周りの関心でした。

題材 TechEd（308件） ASUG（176件）

AI エージェント47%42%
移行（RISE・移行・転換）7%20%
費用・ROI・価値7%18%
ガバナンス10%18%
規制・コンプライアンス5%11%
クリーンコア3%9%
呼び名「BTP」1件22件
呼び名「Business AI Platform」41件13件

（タイトルと概要文に出てくる語で数えたもので、講演の中身そのものではありません）

【📷 図3：fig3-teched-vs-asug.png／Share of sessions by topic, SAP TechEd Berlin vs. ASUG Tech Connect】

 

移行、費用対効果、ガバナンス、規制の比率は、ASUG のほうが2〜3倍高くなっています。顧客の立場の登壇や顧客事例の回も42件あり、食品・消費財の事例も目立ちます。呼び名も、利用者の側ではまだ「BTP」のほうが通じているようです。

昨年 ASUG に参加したときの感覚とも重なるのですが、TechEd が SAP からの「提供側の地図」だとすると、ASUG は「利用側の悩みの地図」に近いと感じます。同じ AI エージェントの話でも、TechEd は「何ができるか」、ASUG は「どう移行して、いくらかかって、どう管理するか」に寄っています。

6. Clean Core と S/4HANA 移行はどう扱われているか

AI エージェント一色に見えるカタログですが、Clean Core や S/4HANA（SAP Cloud ERP）への移行の話がなくなったわけではありません。TechEd には「Accelerate and de-risk transformation（移行・変革）」というトラックがあり、35件あります。

TechEd で目につくのは、移行の作業そのものに AI を使う回です。たとえば次のような回があります。

  • TM105「Agent-led custom code migration: From planning to mass adaptation」（アドオンの移行をエージェントで進める）
  • TM263「AI-accelerated RISE with SAP migration with the system transition workbench」（ハンズオン）
  • TM108「The journey with clean core continues for SAP Cloud ERP Private」
  • XP110「Beyond migration: Turning Neo sunset into strategic platform transformation」（Neo 環境の終了への対応）

ASUG のほうは顧客事例が中心で、どちらかというと「AI を本格的に使うには、まず Clean Core とデータを整える」という順番で語られています。HP・Jabil・Bristol Myers Squibb が登壇する「AI at Scale Starts with a Clean Core」、Florida Crystals が4週間で Clean Core の評価をした事例、Costco の移行の自動化、Hershey の RISE と Business Data Cloud の事例などです。上の表でも、移行の比率は TechEd の7%に対して ASUG は20%、クリーンコアは3%に対して9%でした。

TechEd は「移行を AI で速くする」、ASUG は「AI のために足元を整える」。同じ Clean Core と AI の組み合わせを、提供側と利用側が逆の向きから語っているように見えます。昨年の記事でも Clean Core は両イベントに共通するテーマでしたが、今年は AI と組になって語られるようになっています。

【📷 図4：fig4-opposite-directions.png／Clean core and AI approached from opposite directions at TechEd and ASUG】

 

7. 両トップの最近の発言も、同じ方向を指している

カタログの傾向は、SAP と ASUG のトップの最近の発言とも重なります。

SAP の Christian Klein 氏は、5月の Sapphire の基調講演で、公開データで学習した汎用の LLM だけでは基幹業務には足りないと述べています。消費者向けの AI なら8割の正確さでも許されるが企業ではそうはいかない、という趣旨で、「Eighty percent is just not good enough」と表現しました。データのモデルが壊れていれば、どんなエージェントでも補えない、とも話しています。10月の SAP Connect の記者会見では、文脈（コンテキスト）とガバナンスはセットだと強調し、3年がかりの移行の時代は終わったとも語ったと報じられています。TechEd で AI の運用と保護のトラックが最大になり、Knowledge Graph の回や移行を AI で進める回が並んでいるのは、この方針がそのまま技術の中身になったものと読めます。

一方、昨年の記事でも紹介した ASUG の Geoff Scott 氏は、10月に公開された ASUG の S/4HANA 調査の紹介で、会員の関心は「S/4HANA に移ること」から「S/4HANA で価値を出すこと」に移り、定着やガバナンス、稼働後の取り組みに向いていると話しています。8月のインタビューでは、エージェントは整ったデータに頼るので、顧客や品目をどう定義するかといったマスターデータのガバナンスを、判断を任せる前に決めておく必要があると指摘しました。今は実験することが何より大事だ、とも述べています。ASUG のカタログで移行・費用・ガバナンスの比率が高く、「AI のためにまず足元を整える」顧客事例が並ぶのと、ちょうど同じ向きです。

面白いのは、二人とも「データと文脈とガバナンスが先」という点では一致していることです。違うのはその先で、SAP は「だから SAP の基盤とクラウドで」、ASUG は「だから、まず自分たちのデータを整えよう」と続きます。TechEd と ASUG の違いは、この立ち位置の違いがそのまま出たものなのかもしれません。

8. 日本の会社は登場するか

少し気になって、登壇者の所属も調べてみました。TechEd Berlin では、登壇者（延べ675人）の所属に日本企業は見当たりませんでした。

ASUG Tech Connect では、日本にゆかりのある会社の米国拠点の事例が2つあります。DIC グループの Sun Chemical による API のモダナイゼーションと SAP BTP の事例と、2019年にパナソニックから独立した i-PRO Americas による受注処理の自動化の事例です。i-PRO の回の紹介文には、日本のチームも関心を持っていると書かれています。

ちなみに5月の Sapphire（オーランド）には、ダイキン、富士通、武田薬品などの事例があり、SuccessFactors の基調講演にはトヨタの方も登壇していました。経営と事業の場である Sapphire には日本企業の名前が出てくるのに、技術の場ではまだ少ない。日本のユーザーが技術の話をする側に回れるとよいな、と思います。

9. 私が現地で見てきたいこと

ここからは個人の関心です。私は AI を作る話よりも、作ったものを企業としてどう管理するかに関心があります。今年はちょうど、そこが TechEd の大きな柱になっているので楽しみにしています。具体的には、次のようなことを確かめてきたいと思っています。

  • エージェントの台帳と統制は、SAP 以外のエージェントまでどこまで見られるのか
  • AI の使用量に応じた課金（AI ユニット）は、利用者からどう見えて、どう管理できるのか
  • 移行やアドオンの書き換えをエージェントに任せる話は、実際にどこまで使える段階なのか

ハンズオンでは、AI を使ったサイバーレジリエンスの机上演習（XP160）と、SAP Company Memory のプレビュー（BT162）に参加する予定です。

おわりに

カタログの数字は、あくまで「何が予定されているか」です。会場で実際に何が語られ、参加者が何に反応しているかは、行ってみないと分かりません。

持ち帰った情報のお届けについて

現地で見聞きしたことは、次の2つの場でお届けする予定です。

  • 12月8日（火）JSUG Conference 2026：テクニカル部会のセッション「B-2 SAP最新技術情報の共有～TechEd・ASUG Tech Connect 2026より～」（11:15〜12:00）で、TechEd と ASUG Tech Connect に参加したメンバーが現地の最新情報をお届けします。
    お申し込みはこちら：https://www.jsug.org/conference2026
  • 1月のテクニカル部会：参加したメンバーが、それぞれのテーマをより詳しく紹介します。日程と申込方法は決まりしだい、この記事に追記します。開催後の資料の配布先も、あわせてここでお知らせする予定です。

どちらも JSUG の会員の方であればご参加いただけます。詳細は JSUG のホームページをご覧ください。

この記事で書いたのは、あくまで行く前の「読み」です。実際に確かめてどうだったのか、予想どおりだったところも外れたところも、両方の場で正直にお伝えしたいと思います。ぜひご参加ください。

TechEd は同じ日程でオンライン（SAP TechEd Virtual）でも基調講演と一部のセッションが配信されます。今年は現地に行かない方も、ぜひのぞいてみてください。ベルリンでお会いできる方がいれば、声をかけていただけるとうれしいです。

データについて

  • SAP TechEd Berlin 2026 公式セッションカタログ、ASUG Tech Connect 2026 公式アジェンダ（いずれも2026年10月6日に取得・ログイン不要の公開情報）
  • どちらのカタログも、内容が変わる可能性があると明記しています
  • 本稿は公開情報を集計・整理したもので、SAP・ASUG の公式見解ではありません

[English Version]

Before SAP TechEd Berlin 2026: What I Learned by Counting Every Session in the Catalog

Disclaimer:

This article reflects my personal views as an Opinion Leader of the JSUG Technical SIG and does not represent the official views of JSUG. Generative AI was used to compile the session data and to draft parts of the text. I cannot guarantee the accuracy of the content, so please use the information at your own discretion.

Key points

  • Before attending, I counted every session in the public catalogs of SAP TechEd Berlin 2026 (308 sessions) and ASUG Tech Connect 2026 (176 sessions).
  • AI agents are the main theme of both events (40–50% of sessions). At TechEd, the track on architecting, operating, and securing AI is larger than the track on building agents and apps, and enterprise-wide AI governance has its own track.
  • Joule Work, SAP AI Agent Hub, Joule Studio, and other announcements from SAP Sapphire in May now appear at TechEd as hands-on workshops and customer stories. Anthropic and NVIDIA, however, are not mentioned in the TechEd catalog.
  • At ASUG, migration, cost, governance, and regulation come up two to three times more often than at TechEd. TechEd leans toward "using AI to speed up migration," while ASUG leans toward "getting your foundation ready for AI." Recent remarks by SAP's Christian Klein and ASUG's Geoff Scott point in the same respective directions.
  • What we learn on site will be shared at the JSUG Conference on December 8 and at the JSUG Technical SIG meeting planned for January.

Introduction

SAP TechEd takes place in Berlin from October 27 to 29. A week later, from November 2 to 4, ASUG Tech Connect is held in Fort Worth, Texas. As in previous years, members of the JSUG (Japan SAP Users' Group) Technical SIG will attend both events. I will be going to Berlin.

Last year, I wrote a report after attending ASUG Tech Connect. This year, I decided to write something before I go.

It started as preparation for the trip. I was looking through the public session catalogs to decide which sessions to attend, but there were simply too many to follow by eye. I collected every session from the TechEd and ASUG Tech Connect catalogs and counted them by format, track, and keyword. A few trends emerged that I would not have noticed just by scrolling through the lists.

I hope this gives a useful overview to those attending, those watching online, and those skipping this year. All figures are based on the public catalogs as of October 6.

1. A quick recap: SAP's major events

Many readers will already know this, but here is a brief recap. SAP currently hosts three major events of its own:

  • SAP Sapphire (May): Strategy and business announcements. The Orlando event is held jointly with the ASUG Annual Conference.
  • SAP Connect (October): For line-of-business users. It brought together the separate events for HR, procurement, finance, and other areas into one in 2025.
  • SAP TechEd (October): For IT professionals and technologists.

TechEd also has regional editions (TechEd on Tour), and in North America ASUG Tech Connect plays that role. In Japan, SAP Japan holds the online SAP TechEd Japan, and JSUG sends members to the events and reports back at the JSUG Conference or etc.

2. This year's flow: vision in May, availability in October, then the technical details

At Sapphire in May, SAP introduced the "Autonomous Enterprise" and the SAP Business AI Platform, with a vision of more than 50 assistants and more than 200 agents.

At SAP Connect in early October, SAP announced that general availability of these capabilities is starting. Many of the individual assistants, however, are planned for late 2026 to early 2027.

TechEd comes next in this flow. I see this year's TechEd as the place to find out what the vision presented to executives looks like in technical terms.

【📷 Figure 1：fig1-event-flow.png】

 

3. How Sapphire announcements are taking shape at TechEd

I used the catalog to trace how the Sapphire announcements appear at TechEd. Things that were announcements in May now show up as hands-on workshops and customer stories.

  • Joule Work: The new Joule-centered workspace introduced at Sapphire. It appears in 25 TechEd sessions, including hands-on workshops on the desktop, mobile, and web experiences (JW163, JW164, JW261). JW206 is described as featuring customers who run it in production in manufacturing, retail, and enterprise IT.
  • SAP AI Agent Hub: The agent inventory that Sapphire said would be available in Q3. TechEd offers a hands-on workshop covering agents from discovery to decommissioning (BT161) and a session on how SAP uses it internally (BT116).
  • Joule Studio: The most frequent, appearing in 51 sessions. There are several hands-on workshops for building your own agents, a session on the transition path from SAP Build to Joule Studio (AD106), and a story from the manufacturer Knapp, which is preparing for that transition (ST126).
  • Joule assistants: Hands-on workshops let you try assistants for sourcing (AS264, Sourcing Assistant) and financial closing (AS260, Financial Closing Assistant).
  • SAP Business Data Cloud: A hands-on workshop on sharing data products without copies (DA162) and a Henkel case in which SAP and Adobe agents work together (DA206).

On the other hand, Anthropic (Claude) and NVIDIA, the external partners highlighted at Sapphire, are not mentioned anywhere in the TechEd catalog, and Databricks appears only four times. Not being in the catalog does not mean they will not be covered, but TechEd seems to focus on what SAP's own products can do.

4. Counting the SAP TechEd Berlin 2026 catalog

TechEd Berlin has 308 sessions.

The first thing I noticed is how clear the main theme is. AI agents appear in the title or abstract of 144 sessions, or 47% of the total. The most frequent products are SAP Business AI Platform, Joule, and Joule Studio.

What surprised me was the track structure. Of the nine tracks, the largest is "Architect, operate, and secure AI at scale" with 57 sessions, more than the track for building agents, workflows, and applications (49). "Drive AI governance for enterprise-wide impact" is also a separate track with 27 sessions. Looking inside, you find the agent inventory (SAP AI Agent Hub), monitoring (SAP Cloud ALM), and SAP's own internal operations. The center of gravity seems to be shifting gradually from building AI to managing what has been built.

【📷 Figure 2：fig2-teched-tracks.png】

 

A few points also caught my attention:

  • Very few sessions mention regulation (such as the EU AI Act). Governance is mostly discussed as operational management: inventory, monitoring, cost, and decommissioning.
  • Of the 244 sessions with a speaker type, 232 are SAP. It makes sense to read the TechEd catalog as a map of what SAP is promoting.

By the way, the platform name is also changing. In the TechEd catalog, "SAP Business AI Platform" appears in 41 sessions and "BTP" in only one.

5. Compared with ASUG Tech Connect

ASUG Tech Connect 2026 has 176 sessions (officially 190+, with more added every week). Of these, 44 are repeats with the same titles as TechEd sessions.

AI agents are the main theme here too. The difference is in the surrounding interests.

Topic TechEd (308) ASUG (176)

AI agents47%42%
Migration (RISE, migration, conversion)7%20%
Cost, ROI, value7%18%
Governance10%18%
Regulation, compliance5%11%
Clean core3%9%
Name "BTP"122
Name "Business AI Platform"4113

(Counted by words in titles and abstracts, not by the actual content of the talks.)

【📷 Figure 3：fig3-teched-vs-asug.png】

 

Migration, ROI, governance, and regulation appear two to three times more often at ASUG. There are also 42 sessions with customer speakers or in the customer story format, with many food and consumer goods cases. On the user side, "BTP" still seems to be the more familiar name.

This matches my impression from attending ASUG last year: if TechEd is SAP's "map of what is offered," ASUG is closer to a "map of what users are struggling with." Even on the same topic of AI agents, TechEd leans toward what is possible, and ASUG leans toward how to migrate, how much it costs, and how to manage it.

6. Clean core and S/4HANA migration

The catalogs may look as if they are all about AI agents, but clean core and migration to S/4HANA (SAP Cloud ERP) have not gone away. TechEd has a track called "Accelerate and de-risk transformation" with 35 sessions.

What stands out at TechEd are sessions that use AI for the migration work itself. For example:

  • TM105 "Agent-led custom code migration: From planning to mass adaptation"
  • TM263 "AI-accelerated RISE with SAP migration with the system transition workbench" (hands-on)
  • TM108 "The journey with clean core continues for SAP Cloud ERP Private"
  • XP110 "Beyond migration: Turning Neo sunset into strategic platform transformation"

ASUG is built around customer stories, and the order tends to be "to use AI at scale, first get your clean core and data in shape." Examples include "AI at Scale Starts with a Clean Core" with speakers from HP, Jabil, and Bristol Myers Squibb, Florida Crystals' four-week clean core assessment, Costco's migration automation, and Hershey's RISE and Business Data Cloud journey. In the table above, migration is 7% at TechEd versus 20% at ASUG, and clean core is 3% versus 9%.

TechEd says "use AI to speed up migration," and ASUG says "get your foundation ready for AI." The provider side and the user side seem to approach the same combination of clean core and AI from opposite directions. In last year's article, clean core was a common theme of both events; this year, it is discussed together with AI.

【📷 Figure 4：fig4-opposite-directions.png】

 

7. Recent remarks by both leaders point the same way

The catalog trends also match recent remarks by the leaders of SAP and ASUG.

In his Sapphire keynote in May, SAP's Christian Klein said that general-purpose LLMs trained on public data are not enough for mission-critical business. Consumer AI may get away with 80% accuracy, but businesses cannot, as he put it: "Eighty percent is just not good enough." He also said that no agent can make up for a broken data model. At the SAP Connect press Q&A in October, he reportedly stressed that context and governance go together and declared the end of three-year migrations. The fact that the AI operations and security track is the largest at TechEd, alongside sessions on the Knowledge Graph and AI-driven migration, can be read as this direction turning into technical content.

Meanwhile, ASUG's Geoff Scott, whom I also quoted in last year's article, said in October, when ASUG's S/4HANA research was published, that members' attention has shifted from getting to S/4HANA to getting value from it, with a focus on adoption, governance, and post-go-live work. In an interview in August, he pointed out that agents depend on clean, consistent data, so companies need to decide how to govern master data, such as how to define a customer or a product, before they hand decisions over to agents. He also said that experimenting is the most important thing right now. This fits well with the higher share of migration, cost, and governance in the ASUG catalog and its customer stories about getting the foundation ready for AI.

What I find interesting is that both agree that data, context, and governance come first. The difference is what follows. SAP continues with "so use SAP's platform and the cloud," while ASUG continues with "so let's get our own data in order first." The difference between TechEd and ASUG may simply reflect this difference in standpoint.

8. Do Japanese companies appear?

Out of curiosity, I also checked the speakers' companies. At TechEd Berlin, I found no Japanese companies among the speakers (675 speaker slots in total).

At ASUG Tech Connect, there are two sessions from US operations of companies with Japanese roots: Sun Chemical, part of the DIC Group, on API modernization and SAP BTP, and i-PRO Americas, which became independent from Panasonic in 2019, on automating order processing. The i-PRO session description mentions that its team in Japan is also interested.

By contrast, Sapphire Orlando in May included cases from Daikin, Fujitsu, and Takeda, and a speaker from Toyota appeared in the SuccessFactors keynote. Japanese companies show up at Sapphire, the business-focused event, but are still rare at the technical events. I hope more Japanese users will take the stage to talk about technology.

9. What I want to see on site

This part is my personal interest. I am more interested in how companies manage AI than in how they build it. This year, that happens to be one of TechEd's main pillars, so I am looking forward to it. Specifically, I want to find out:

  • How far the agent inventory and governance can see, including non-SAP agents
  • How usage-based pricing for AI (AI Units) looks to users and how it can be managed
  • How ready, in practice, it is to hand migration and custom code rework over to agents

For hands-on workshops, I plan to join the AI-enabled tabletop exercise for cyber resilience (XP160) and the SAP Company Memory preview (BT162).

Closing

The numbers in the catalog only show what is planned. What is actually said on stage and what attendees react to can only be seen on site.

Sharing what we bring back

We plan to share what we see and hear at the following two events:

  • JSUG Conference 2026, Tuesday, December 8: In the Technical SIG session "B-2: Sharing the Latest SAP Technology Updates from SAP TechEd and ASUG Tech Connect 2026" (11:15–12:00, in Japanese), members who attended TechEd and ASUG Tech Connect will share the latest information from the events.
    Registration: https://www.jsug.org/conference2026
  • JSUG Technical SIG meeting in January: Attending members will cover their topics in more detail. I will add the date and registration information to this article once they are announced, along with a link to the materials after the meeting.

Both events are open to JSUG members. Please see the JSUG website for details.

What I wrote here is only my reading before the event. I want to share honestly at both events what turned out as expected and what did not. I hope you can join us.

TechEd keynotes and some sessions will also be streamed online on the same dates (SAP TechEd Virtual), so please take a look even if you are not going this year. If you will be in Berlin, I would be happy if you said hello.

About the data

  • SAP TechEd Berlin 2026 official session catalog and ASUG Tech Connect 2026 official agenda (both retrieved on October 6, 2026; public information available without login)
  • Both catalogs state that their content is subject to change
  • This article compiles and organizes public information and does not represent the official views of SAP or ASUG

entry.title: Natural Language (NL) Over SAP Data: A Practical MCP Pattern for Joule Desktop & Pro-Code Agent
entry.content:
Introduction

Any S/4HANA OData API, standard or custom, can be exposed as an MCP server through SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway and consumed by AI agents through two complementary paths: Joule Work Desktop for a direct, low-overhead experience, and a custom agent in Cloud Foundry that can be triggered in Joule SAP Build Work Zone for an orchestrated, reasoning-capable experience. 

To make it concrete, we applied it to SAP Production Revenue Accounting (PRA) data: a domain that is rich, complex, and mission-critical, and where the gap between the data and the people who need it is wide enough to make the pattern's value immediately visible. The solution is not PRA-specific. The same architecture applies to any standard or custom OData V4 service in S/4HANA: Finance, Plant Maintenance, Materials Management, Sales and Distribution, or any domain where business users need structured answers without writing queries or navigating transaction codes.

This blog walks through the architecture, the components, the implementation decisions, and the trade-offs behind the two access patterns we designed and deployed:

  1. Joule Work Desktop — connects directly to an custom MCP server published via SAP Integration Suite. Ideal for business users who want a direct AI interface to standard PRA revenue accounting tables.

  2. Joule in SAP Build Work Zone — routes through a custom AI agent on SAP Cloud Foundry that adds an intelligent reasoning layer. Ideal for business users already operating inside Work Zone.

Both patterns share the same backend: a custom OData V4 service exposing standard SAP PRA tables, published as an MCP server through SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway.

A full end-to-end walkthrough has been recorded as a companion to this blog.

Solution Architecture

The architecture is deliberately generic. Swap out the PRA OData service for any other S/4HANA OData V4 endpoint and the rest of the pattern holds unchanged.

The solution exposes standard S/4HANA PRA tables via a custom OData V4 service (built on ABAP RAP), publishes them as governed MCP tools through SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway, and surfaces them to business users via natural language either directly through Joule Work Desktop or through a custom AI agent embedded in SAP Build Work Zone.

Path 1 — Joule Desktop:

Desktop User → Joule Desktop → MCP → SAP Integration Suite → OData → S/4HANA

Path 2 — Joule in Work Zone:

Web User → SAP Build Work Zone (Joule) → A2A → Custom Agent on CF → MCP → SAP Integration Suite → OData → S/4HANA

Component Walkthrough

1. S/4HANA On-Premise — The Data Source

The data lives in a standard S/4HANA on-premise system. We exposed the standard PRA tables via a custom OData V4 service built using the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP).

The service exposes all 13 entity sets with proper navigation associations, enabling deep $expand queries across both the Document and Revenue Distribution branches. 

 

2. SAP Integration Suite — MCP Gateway

This is the integration layer that bridges the RAP OData service into the AI world.

SAP Integration Suite's MCP Server capability (part of the MCP Gateway feature, available with the Premium subscription) consumes the OData V4 service metadata and automatically generates MCP tool definitions for every operation. For our 13-entity service, this produced 41 MCP tools covering list queries, filtered reads, and navigation operations.

Why MCP? The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for AI tool discovery and invocation. By publishing our OData service as an MCP server, we make it consumable by any MCP-compatible client, including Joule Work Desktop, LangChain agents, or any future client, without changing the backend.

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

The Developer Hub within Integration Suite is used to publish the MCP server, generating the OAuth credentials that clients use to authenticate. It also provides discoverability within the organization: other developers can find and reuse the same MCP server without rebuilding the integration from scratch.

3. SAP Cloud Foundry — Custom Reasoning Agent

For the Work Zone path, we built a custom Python agent deployed on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry. This agent adds the reasoning layer that bridges Joule's natural language input to structured MCP tool calls.

The agent stack:

ComponentRole

a2a-sdk

Implements the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, exposing a JSON-RPC 2.0 endpoint that Joule can call

LangGraph + LangChain

ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) loop: decides which MCP tools to call, in what order, based on the user's question

langchain-mcp-adapters

Loads MCP tools from Integration Suite at runtime and wraps them as LangChain 

LiteLLM / langchain-litellm

Routes LLM calls to SAP AI Core using the standard OpenAI-compatible interface

The ReAct pattern is important here. Rather than a single-shot query, the agent reasons iteratively: it reads the question, identifies which MCP tools are relevant, calls them, evaluates the results, and decides whether additional calls are needed before formulating the final answer. This is what makes it capable of answering multi-hop questions that require joining data from multiple PRA tables.

4. Registering the A2A Agent with Joule

Deployment uses the Joule CLI. The deploy command registers the custom agent as a Joule capability. By default, this deploys to standalone Joule.

To surface the agent inside SAP Build Work Zone, update the assistant type to sap_digital_Assistant. The Joule Admin Center (accessible by appending /admin to the Joule instance URL) allows you to verify the deployment and confirm the capability is active.

5. SAP Build Work Zone - Registering the A2A Agent with Joule

SAP Build Work Zone is the standard business user entry point. Joule is embedded natively in the Work Zone shell,  no separate app to open, no separate login.

6. Joule Work Desktop Experience

For users who prefer the Joule Work Desktop standalone experience, the integration is simpler: Joule Work Desktop connects directly to the MCP server. No custom agent, no A2A, no Cloud Foundry deployment required.

Conclusion

The architecture supports two distinct experiences from the same foundation. Joule Work Desktop connects directly to the MCP server no agent required giving business users a fast, lightweight path to query SAP data in natural language. Joule in SAP Build Work Zone routes through a custom AI agent deployed on BTP Cloud Foundry, adding multi-step reasoning, tool orchestration, and a governed conversational interface for broader business user adoption.

The architecture is composable by design. The OData V4 service, MCP server, reasoning agent, and Joule capability are independent layers each doing one thing well. Swap the data source and the pattern applies to any SAP domain. Complexity lives where it belongs: the OData layer owns the data model, MCP handles tool discoverability, LangGraph handles reasoning, and Joule handles the conversation.

Consider which of your OData APIs could benefit from this pattern  a Finance posting service, a Plant Maintenance feed, a Sales Order status endpoint. Any of them can become a natural language interface using exactly this stack.

entry.title: The Evolution of the SAP User Interface: From SAP GUI to Fiori to Joule Work
entry.content:
The Evolution of the SAP User Interface: From SAP GUI to Fiori to Joule Work

From transactions to intuitive apps to AI-powered collaboration – the SAP user experience is not just changing its appearance. It is changing the way we work.

Anyone who has worked with SAP for a long time will remember it: the classic SAP GUI, countless transaction codes, complex screens, and a user interface that was primarily designed to do one thing – provide functionality.

But the world has changed. And so have our expectations of enterprise software.

Looking back, we can see just how far we have come – and what this evolution means for us as people.

1. SAP GUI – The Era of Transactions

Throughout the 1990s and well beyond, SAP GUI was the central entry point to business processes in countless companies.

The interface was powerful, stable, and designed to support complex business processes. To use SAP efficiently, users had to become familiar with transaction codes, screens, fields, and process logic.

People had to learn how SAP worked.

Over the years, experienced users developed an enormous amount of knowledge. They knew which transaction to use, which fields mattered, and which steps were required to achieve the desired result.

It worked – but shift began in the design of the user experience.

Instead of complex transaction screens, the focus moved towards role-based apps, modern design, and more intuitive interaction. The user experience became increasingly aligned with people's tasks and needs.

Information was meant to be easier to access. Processes were meant to become more understandable. And SAP was increasingly expected to feel as intuitive as the modern applications we use in everyday life.

The key question changed: Not just “How does this transaction work?” but “What task do I want to accomplish?”

With Fiori, access to SAP became more modern, flexible, and better suited to different roles and devices.

This was more than a new design. It was an important step towards a better user experience and a stronger focus on people.

3. Joule Work – From Using Software to AI-Powered Collaboration

With generative AI, the next chapter of the SAP user experience is beginning.

AI assistants such as Joule make it possible to ask for information in natural language, understand relationships more quickly, and receive intelligent support when completing certain tasks.

With Joule Work, SAP is taking this approach further towards an AI-powered work environment. The aim is to bring information and work contexts together more effectively and support tasks across different applications and business processes.

Instead of navigating exclusively through menus and applications, users can increasingly describe what they want to achieve.

Imagine a typical business scenario:

Instead of opening multiple reports and manually compiling data, a user could ask:

“Analyze sales performance over the past three months, identify the largest deviations, and summarize the most important areas for action.”

The vision is for AI to help users find information, analyze data, and prepare decisions – and, depending on available capabilities and permissions, also assist in executing tasks.

People will spend less time searching for information and more time interpreting it and making the right decisions.

An important point: Not every task can already be fully automated. The actual benefits depend on the available capabilities, integration with business processes, and the quality of the underlying data.

4. The Real Change Is About People

The evolution of the SAP user interface is therefore not just a story about technology.

It is also a story about how our work is changing.

Era What matters most What it means for people

SAP GUITransactions and screensSystem knowledge and process expertise are essential
SAP FioriApps and tasksMore intuitive interaction and easier access to information
Joule Work and AIIntent, context, and assistanceGreater focus on analysis, decisions, and collaboration

This evolution raises important questions.

Which skills will become more important in the future?

Knowledge of individual transactions will remain valuable in many areas. At the same time, other skills will become increasingly important: asking the right questions, critically evaluating results, understanding business processes, and using AI effectively.

The roles of IT departments, SAP consultants, and process owners are also changing. It is no longer just about configuring systems correctly and training users. Increasingly, it is about designing intelligent workflows, making meaningful use of data, and helping people adapt to a new world of work.

And this is where a major challenge lies: New technology alone does not change the way people work. Real value is created only when people understand, trust, and use it effectively.

5. What Does This Mean for SAP Transformations?

For companies, one important insight emerges: The evolution of the user interface should not be treated as an isolated IT project.

Organizations modernizing SAP should also rethink their workflows, employee roles, data quality, and opportunities for automation.

Some key questions to consider:

  • Which tasks can be simplified through better user experience and guidance?

  • Where can AI assistants make information available more quickly?

  • Which processes are suitable for further automation?

  • How can we ensure that employees understand and embrace the new possibilities?

  • How do we measure whether productivity, quality, and employee satisfaction are actually improving?

Especially in the SAP ecosystem, it will be crucial to develop technology, processes, and people together.

Because a modern interface is not an end in itself. It must make work easier, better, and more meaningful.

Conclusion: Less Time Operating Systems. More Time Making an Impact.

From SAP GUI through SAP Fiori to Joule Work, we are witnessing an evolution that goes far beyond the design of a user interface.

We are moving from a world where people had to learn how to operate the system, through a world of intuitive, task-oriented applications, towards a way of working in which AI increasingly understands, assists, and supports tasks.

The exciting question is therefore no longer just what the next SAP interface will look like.

The real question is: How much more can people achieve when technology takes some of the complexity off their shoulders?

The future of SAP will not be measured solely by how intelligent the systems become. It will be measured by how effectively they help people make better decisions, collaborate more efficiently, and focus on what truly matters.

Less complexity. More intelligence. More time for what really matters.
